Case Number: 22BBCV00730    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

(CONTINUED FROM AUGUST 21, 2026) 

MOTION TO QUASH SUBPOENAS

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 22BBCV00730

 

MP:     Plaintiff Anait Basmadzhyan

RP:      Defendant City of Los Angeles

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS:

 

A.     Operative Complaint

 

Anait Basmadzhyan (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on January 29, 2022, Plaintiff was injured from an uneven sidewalk which contained cracked and unmaintained materials constituting a dangerous condition on public property. 

 

The Complaint, filed October 10, 2022, alleges a single cause of action against Defendants City of Los Angeles (“City”) and County of Los Angeles (“County”) for Statutory Liability for Dangerous Condition of Public Property against Public Entities and Employees (Govt. Code, §§ 815.2(a), 820(a), 835, 840.2, and 840.4). 

 

On January 3, 2023, Plaintiff dismissed County without prejudice. 

 

B.     Operative Cross-Complaint

 

On March 7, 2023, City filed a cross-complaint against Roes 1-10 for: (1) Indemnification; (2) Apportionment of Fault; and (3) Declaratory Relief.

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On July 17, 2026, Plaintiff Anait Basmadzhyan filed a Motion to Quash Subpoenas for Medical, Radiology, and Billing.  On August 6, 2026, City filed an opposition.  On August 14, 2026, Plaintiff filed a reply.

 

The matter initially came on hearing on August 21, 2026.  The Court continued the hearing to September 4, 2026 so that all parties may be present for oral argument.  On September 3, 2026, the Court granted the parties’ stipulation to continue the hearing to September 11, 2026. 

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

C.C.P.  § 1987.1 grants the trial court authority to quash a subpoena when necessary.  C.C.P. § 1987.1(a) states, “If a subpoena requires the attendance of a witness or the production of books, documents, or other things before a court, or at the trial of an issue therein, or at the taking of a deposition, the court, upon motion reasonably made by any person described in subdivision (b), or upon the court’s own motion after giving counsel notice and an opportunity to be heard, may make an order quashing the subpoena entirely, modifying it, or directing compliance with it upon those terms or conditions as the court shall declare, including protective orders.  In addition, the court may make any other order as may be appropriate to protect the person from unreasonable or oppressive demands, including unreasonable violations of the right of privacy of the person.”  

 

C.C.P. § 2017.020(a) states: “The court shall limit the scope of discovery if it determines that the burden, expense, or intrusiveness of that discovery clearly outweighs the likelihood that the information sought will lead to the discovery of admissible evidence. The court may make this determination pursuant to a motion for protective order by a party or other affected person. This motion shall be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration under Section 2016.040.”

 

ANALYSIS:  

 

Plaintiff seeks an order quashing or modifying the City’s subpoenas to limit production from five years before the January 29, 2022 incident (January 29, 2017) to the present, or alternatively: (a) production of records in the first instance to Plaintiff’s counsel who shall produce all responsive records to City and serve a log of withheld documents within 15 days; or (b) an in camera review; and (c) a protective order limiting the use of the produced records to this action.  City’s eight medical, billing, and radiology records subpoenas issued on June 23, 2026, include: 

 

·         (1) Kaiser Permanente – Central ROI Unit (Medical Records) [Ref # 145276-01], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital medical records including but not limited to both private and industrial records, doctors notes, treatment and evaluation records, nurses notes, inpatient and outpatient records, correspondence, lab results, diagnostic test results and all medical and radiology reports.”

 

·         (2) Kaiser Permanente – Central ROI Unit (Billing Records) [Ref # 145276-02], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital itemized billing records.”

 

·         (3) Kaiser Permanente (Radiology Dept/Release of Information) (Radiology Records) [Ref # 145276-03], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital X-rays, MRI’s and CT scans and reports.”

 

·         (4) Dr. Marina Gold at 800 Central Avenue, Suite 305 in Glendale (Medical, Billing, and Radiology Records) [Ref # 145276-04], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital MEDICAL and ITEMIZED BILLING records including but not limited to both private and industrial records, doctors notes, nurses notes, inpatient and outpatient records, correspondence, lab results, diagnostic test results and all medical and radiology reports. To include and and[sic] all actual X-RAY FILMS, CT & MRI SCANS on CD ONLY.”

 

·         (5) Dr. Marina Gold at 631 E. Colorado Street in Glendale (Medical, Billing, and Radiology Records) [Ref # 145276-05], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital MEDICAL and ITEMIZED BILLING records including but not limited to both private and industrial records, doctors notes, nurses notes, inpatient and outpatient records, correspondence, lab results, diagnostic test results and all medical and radiology reports. To include and and[sic] all actual X-RAY FILMS, CT & MRI SCANS on CD ONLY.” 

 

·         (6) Adventist Health Glendale (Medical Records) [Ref # 145276-06], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital medical records including but not limited to both private and industrial records, doctors notes, treatment and evaluation records, nurses notes, inpatient and outpatient records, correspondence, lab results, diagnostic test results and all medical and radiology reports. [¶] To include any and all records from Dr. Anna Lafia.” 

 

·         (7) Adventist Health Glendale (Billing Records) including records of Dr. Anna Lafia [Ref # 145276-07], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital itemized billing records. [¶] To include any and all records from Dr. Anna Lafia.” 

 

·         (8) Adventist Health Glendale (Radiology) including records of Dr. Anna Lafia [Ref # 145276-08], seeking: “Any and all non-privileged physical and digital X-rays, MRI’s and CT scans and reports. [¶] To include any and all records from Dr. Anna Lafia.” 

 

(Petrosyan Decl., Ex. C [Subpoenas].)  On July 17, 2026, Plaintiff objected to the subpoenas.  (Id., Ex. D [Objection].)  The parties attempted to meet and confer regarding temporal limitations to body parts listed in Plaintiff’s discovery responses, prior to Plaintiff filing this motion.  (Id., ¶5, Ex. E.)

 

First, the subpoenas do not include any temporal restrictions such that they potentially seek a lifetime of records.  The parties attempted to meet and confer on this issue and were unable to reach a resolution.  While Plaintiff offers five years prior to the January 29, 2022 subject incident (or January 29, 2017) to the present, City argues that Plaintiff testified in her deposition that she was diagnosed with neuropathy approximately five or six years prior to the incident (Opp. at p.4).  City argues that Plaintiff’s temporal restriction of five years in the motion “are appropriate,” but that Plaintiff’s attempt to further limit the scope of the subpoenas is not supported because Plaintiff claims mental, emotional, physical/orthopedic injuries.  (Opp. at 8:11-17.)  (Differently, on page 11 of the opposition, City appears to seek ten years of pre-incident records irrespective of body parts.)  

 

The Court finds that a six-year temporal limitation is appropriate for this case.  Thus, the subpoenas shall be modified to limit production from records dating January 29, 2016 (six years prior to the January 29, 2022 incident) to the present. 

 

Second, while a plaintiff is not obligated to sacrifice all privacy to seek redress for a specific physical, mental, or emotional injury, “they may not withhold information which relates to any physical or mental condition which they have put in issue by bringing this lawsuit.”  (Britt v. Superior Court (1978) 20 Cal.3d 844, 864; City & County of San Francisco v. Superior Court (1951) 37 Cal.2d 227, 232.)  A plaintiff suing for personal injuries waives the physician-patient privilege to some extent, but this does not make discoverable all of a plaintiff’s lifetime medical history.  (Britt, supra, 20 Cal.3d at 863-64.) 

 

Plaintiff claims the following injuries attributed to the subject incident: the right little and ring fingers (fifth and fourth) fingers; the right hand, wrist, and shoulder; knees; hamstring; thighs; and emotional injury, sleep disruption, anxiety, and depression.  (Petrosyan Decl., Ex. A [Pl.’s FROG 6.3 Response].)  Although City argues that given Plaintiff’s own uncertainty during her deposition regarding her various orthopedic and psychological/emotional injuries, Plaintiff’s withholding of documents about pre-incident medical providers, and its dispute regarding causation and extent of Plaintiff’s injuries, City argues it is entitled to seek medical records/history relevant to the similar body parts alleged in her own discovery responses.  (Opp. at 7:12-16.) 

 

The Court declines to allow discovery to all medical records irrespective of body parts.  As stated in Britt, the Court will limit the subpoenas to the specific body parts that Plaintiff claimed was injured as a result of the subject incident.

 

Finally, Plaintiff requests that if the Court is inclined to permit production beyond the five-year window, then she seeks alternative relief regarding the “first look,” producing records and a redaction log to City, and that all records be used solely for the purposes of this litigation and destroyed/returned at its conclusion.  (Mot. at p.9.)

 

As acknowledged by both Gary Petrosyan (Plaintiff’s counsel) and Jaime Hernandez (defense counsel), Kaiser does not generally parse out medical records based on agreed upon body parts as requested in a subpoena.  (See Petrosyan Decl., Ex. E [July 13 and 15, 2026 Emails].)  In order to protect the physician-patient privilege for body parts that are not at issue in this action, the Court will allow Plaintiff’s counsel to have a “first look” of the subpoenaed documents and provide a privilege log for any redacted documents. 

 

The motion is granted such that the subpoenas shall be modified and limited to no more than six years prior to the subject incident (January 29, 2016) to the present, to the body parts Plaintiff claims were injured as a result of the incident (the right fifth/little and fourth/ring fingers; the right hand, wrist, and shoulder; knees; hamstring; thighs; and emotional injury, sleep disruption, anxiety, and depression).  Based on the parties’ general understanding of Kaiser’s (and perhaps other medical professional’s) practice of not redacting/limiting production of documents, the Court finds Plaintiff’s request for a “first look” of the produced documents to be reasonable in light of Plaintiff’s offer to provide a privilege log for redacted/removed documents. 

 

A.     Sanctions

 

“[I]n making an order pursuant to motion made under subdivision (c) of Section 1987 or under Section 1987.1, the court may in its discretion award the amount of the reasonable expenses incurred in making or opposing the motion, including reasonable attorney's fees, if the court finds the motion was made or opposed in bad faith or without substantial justification or that one or more of the requirements of the subpoena was oppressive.”  (C.C.P.  § 1987.2(a).) 

 

Plaintiff seeks $3,660 in sanctions (= [4 hours on the motion + 5 anticipated hours to review and reply to the opposition and attend the hearing, at $400/hour] + $60 filing fees).  (Petrosyan Decl., ¶9.) 

 

City argues that sanctions should not be ordered because sanctions were not noticed in the motion, there is no declaration supporting sanctions, City offered to modify the subpoenas (to ten years), and Plaintiff filed this motion in bad faith. 

 

Based on the Court’s review of the notice of motion, it states on page 3, lines 9-12 that Plaintiff is requesting monetary sanctions against City and its counsel of record, jointly and severally, in the amount of $3,660 pursuant to C.C.P. § 1987.2.  As such, the notice is sufficient.  Next, counsel Gary Petrosyan’s declaration at paragraph 9 details the time spent, his hourly rate, his anticipated hours, and the filing fee.  (See Petrosyan Decl., ¶9.) 

 

The Court does not find that this motion was filed in bad faith.  Based on a review of the parties’ meet and confer efforts, the parties discussed and offered various proposals on limiting the deposition subpoenas, such that there were good faith meet and confer efforts; however, the parties reached an impasse, resulting in this motion.  Ultimately, Plaintiff was meritorious in bringing this motion, but sanctions are not warranted.

 

Sanctions are denied.

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event the parties submit on this tentative ruling, or a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Plaintiff Anait Basmadzhyan’s Motion to Quash Subpoenas for Medical, Radiology, and Billing came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows: 

 

The Motion TO QUASH OR MODIFY DEFENDANT’S DEPOSITION SUBPOENAS IS GRANTED such that THE SUBPOENAS SHALL BE MODIFIED AND LIMITED TO NO MORE THAN SIX YEARS PRIOR TO THE SUBJECT INCIDENT (OR JANUARY 29, 2016) TO THE PRESENT AND TO THE BODY PARTS PLAINTIFF CLAIMS WERE INJURED AS A RESULT OF THE INCIDENT (THE RIGHT FIFTH/LITTLE AND FOURTH/RING FINGERS; THE RIGHT HAND, WRIST, AND SHOULDER; KNEES; HAMSTRING; THIGHS; AND EMOTIONAL INJURY, SLEEP DISRUPTION, ANXIETY, AND DEPRESSION).   CITY SHALL MODIFY AND REISSUE THE DEPOSITION SUBPOENAS CONSISTENT WITH THESE LIMITATIONS.

 

PLAINTIFF’S COUNSEL SHALL HAVE A “FIRST LOOK” OF THE DOCUMENTS AND MUST NOTIFY DEFENDANT WHEN THE DOCUMENTS HAVE BEEN PRODUCED.  FROM THE DATE OF PRODUCTION, PLAINTIFF SHALL HAVE 14 DAYS TO REVIEW, REDACT, AND CREATE A PRIVILEGE LOG AND SHALL SERVE THE REDACTED DOCUMENTS AND ACCOMPANYING PRIVILEGE LOG BY THE END OF THE 14-DAY DEADLINE. 

 

SANCTIONS ARE DENIED.

 

PLAINTIFF TO PROVIDE NOTICE.  

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.  


Case Number: 24BBCV00244    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

MOTION FOR RECONSIDERATION

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 24BBCV00244

 

MP:     Defendant Gary English

RP:      Plaintiff Judy Choi

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Judy Choi (“Plaintiff”) alleges she contracted with Gary English and Gary English Construction (“Defendants”) to build an Alternative Dwelling Unit (“ADU”) on her property. Plaintiff alleges that despite payment made to Defendants, the project remained unfinished and much of the work that was completed was defective.

 

The Complaint, filed January 29, 2024, alleges: (1) Breach of Contract; (2) Fraud; (3) Unfair Business Practices; (4) Accounting; and (5) Rescission.

 

On June 11, 2024, Defendants filed a cross-complaint against Plaintiff for: (1) Breach of Contract; (2) Quantum Meruit; and (3) Reasonable Value of Work, Labor, Services, and Materials Furnished. 

 

RELEVANT BACKGROUND AND MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 24, 2026, the Court granted Plaintiff’s unopposed motion to compel Defendant’s initial responses to Form Interrogatories (“FROG”), set two and motion for order deeming Requests for Admissions (“RFA”), set two, admitted; ordered responses to the FROG within 30 days; and imposed $2,120 in sanctions against Defendant and his counsel of record payable within 30 days. 

 

On May 6, 2026, Defendant filed a Motion for Reconsideration of the Court Order Deeming RFAs Admitted and/or Alternative Motion for Relief Under C.C.P. §§ 473(b) and 2033.300.  On August 26, 2026, Plaintiff filed an opposition.  On September 3, 2026, Defendant filed a reply.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

C.C.P. § 1008(a) states: “(a) When an application for an order has been made to a judge, or to a court, and refused in whole or in part, or granted, or granted conditionally, or on terms, any party affected by the order may, within 10 days after service upon the party of written notice of entry of the order and based upon new or different facts, circumstances, or law, make application to the same judge or court that made the order, to reconsider the matter and modify, amend, or revoke the prior order. The party making the application shall state by affidavit what application was made before, when and to what judge, what order or decisions were made, and what new or different facts, circumstances, or law are claimed to be shown.”

 

C.C.P. § 2033.300 states:

 

(a) A party may withdraw or amend an admission made in response to a request for admission only on leave of court granted after notice to all parties.

 

(b) The court may permit withdrawal or amendment of an admission only if it determines that the admission was the result of mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect, and that the party who obtained the admission will not be substantially prejudiced in maintaining that party's action or defense on the merits.

 

(c) The court may impose conditions on the granting of the motion that are just, including, but not limited to, the following:

 

(1) An order that the party who obtained the admission be permitted to pursue additional discovery related to the matter involved in the withdrawn or amended admission.

 

(2) An order that the costs of any additional discovery be borne in whole or in part by the party withdrawing or amending the admission.

 

(C.C.P. § 2033.300.) 

 

The mandatory provision of C.C.P. § 473(b) states:

Notwithstanding any other requirements of this section, the court shall, whenever an application for relief is made no more than six months after entry of judgment, is in proper form, and is accompanied by an attorney's sworn affidavit attesting to the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect, vacate any (1) resulting default entered by the clerk against the attorney's client, and which will result in entry of a default judgment, or (2) resulting default judgment or dismissal entered against the attorney's client, unless the court finds that the default or dismissal was not in fact caused by the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect. The court shall, whenever relief is granted based on an attorney's affidavit of fault, direct the attorney to pay reasonable compensatory legal fees and costs to opposing counsel or parties.

 

(C.C.P. § 473(b).)

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     Discussion of Substantive Merits of the Motion

 

Defendant moves for reconsideration, arguing that he served verified, code-complaint responses to the RFA on March 17, 2026, over a month prior to the hearing on the underlying motion to deem the RFAs admitted. 

 

In support of the motion, defense counsel Nick M. Campbell provides his declaration.  Mr. Campbell states that on March 17, 2026, he served via email Defendant’s RFA, set two, responses, without objection, to Plaintiff’s counsel Eugene "Chip" Matthews, at his correct email address, which he used in prior correspondence and which appears on his pleadings.   (Campbell Decl., ¶3.)  Exhibit A includes a March 17, 2026 email from Mr. Campbell to Mr. Matthews attaching Defendant’s RFA and FROG responses were attached.  (Id., ¶3, Ex. A.)  Exhibit B includes the RFA responses, signed by counsel on January 19, 2026 and verified by Defendant that same day.  (Id., ¶3, Ex. B.)  Mr. Campbell states that the March 17, 2026 email did not generate any bounce-back, delivery failure, or undeliverable notice; it was sent with a “high importance” designation; and he had invited Plaintiff’s counsel to meet and confer regarding the pending discovery motions but did not receive a response.  (Id., ¶3.)  At the April 24, 2026 hearing, Plaintiff’s counsel represented to the Court that no responses had been received.  (Id., ¶4.)  Mr. Campbell states that after the hearing, he reviewed his March 17, 2026 email and confirmed the responses had been sent and he forwarded the same to Plaintiff’s counsel.  (Id., ¶4, Ex. C.)  On April 28, 2026, Mr. Campbell again emailed Plaintiff’s counsel by replying directly to a prior email from him, informing Mr. Matthews about the March 17, 2026 email responses and asking if he would be willing to stipulate to set aside the order deeming the RFAs admitted.  (Id., ¶5, Ex. D.)  He states that he has not received any response from Plaintiff’s counsel.  (Id., ¶6.) 

 

Mr. Campbell states that his failure to oppose the underlying motion to deem the RFAs admitted was a result of his mistake and excusable neglect because from September 2025 to early 2026, his office experienced significant technological disruptions, including a mass email chain incident and subsequent system compromises that impacted email functionality and calendaring systems.  (Id., ¶7.)  He states that his office reinstalled email and practice management systems, as well as re-calendared matters, and he inadvertently failed to properly calendar the deadline to the motion to deem the RFAs admitted.  (Id.)  He contends that Plaintiff has not suffered any prejudice as a result of the timing of Defendant’s responses since Plaintiff has been in possession of the verified responses since March 17, 2026 and again when they were re-served after the hearing.  (Id., ¶8.) 

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Mr. Campbell’s declaration lacks credibility and is inconsistent because he attended the April 24, 2026 hearing but failed to present documents regarding service of the RFAs, he has disregarded Court orders and/or refused to comply with discovery rules and has been sanctioned monetarily in the past. 

 

The Court does not find Plaintiff’s arguments persuasive.  At the April 24, 2026 hearing, Mr. Campbell presented oral arguments similar to those made in his declaration but, as he did not file a written opposition and Mr. Campbell did not prepare evidentiary proof at that time to show whether he had in fact served RFA responses, the Court granted the underlying RFA motion but allowed Defendant to file a motion for reconsideration in the event he had documentary proof that the RFAs had indeed been served prior to the hearing.

 

Based on the Court’s review of Mr. Campbell’s email sent on March 17, 2026, Defendant has now provided evidence showing that Defendant served RFA responses prior to the April 24, 2026 hearing.  Thus, Defendant has presented new or different facts and circumstances, showing that responses were provided prior to the hearing.  (See C.C.P. § 2033.280(c) [“The court shall make this order [deeming admitted the truth of any matters specific in the requests], unless it finds that the party to whom the requests for admission have been directed has served, before the hearing on the motion, a proposed response to the requests for admission that is in substantial compliance with Section 2033.220.”].)  A review of the RFA responses show that they were verified, code-compliant responses admitting or denying the matters. 

 

Plaintiff’s counsel Eugene E. Matthews states that he conducted an email search for the RFA responses, but did not find the RFA email.  (Matthews Decl., ¶¶5-6.)  Although Mr. Matthews did not find the March 17, 2026 email in his account, Mr. Campbell’s exhibits show that he did send an email on March 17, 2026 with an RFA attachment without any bounce-back error.  Though inconvenient to Plaintiff, the Court recognizes that there may be technological issues concerning emails—much in the same way that posted mail may have gotten lost during physical delivery.  In light of this unique circumstance, the Court grants this motion for reconsideration.   

 

As the motion is granted pursuant to C.C.P. § 1008, the Court need not address the alternative motion pursuant to C.C.P. § 473(b)’s mandatory provision based on attorney fault. 

 

B.     Sanctions

 

Plaintiff requests that if the motion is granted based on attorney fault under section 473(b), then the Court impose: (1) $3,375 in sanctions for attorney’s fees incurred for opposing this motion (4.5 hours at $750/hour), and (2) $1,500 in sanctions pursuant to the Court’s October 3, 2025 order and $2,120 in sanctions pursuant to the Court’s April 24, 2026 order against Defendant and his counsel of record. 

 

The Court declines to re-impose the $1,500 and/or $2,120 sanctions amounts.  With respect to the $3,375 in sanctions, section 473(c)(1) states: “Whenever the court grants relief from a default, default judgment, or dismissal based on any of the provisions of this section, the court may” impose a penalty upon the offending attorney or party, direct the offending attorney to pay an amount to the State Bar Client Security Fund, or grant other relief as is appropriate.  As noted above, the motion is granted based on section 1008.  As such, the Court need not apply section 473(b)’s provision in ruling on this motion.   

 

C.     Reconsideration

 

For these reasons, the motion for reconsideration is granted.  The Court now reconsiders its April 24, 2026 order and denies Plaintiff’s Motion for Order Deeming RFA, set two, Admitted against Defendant, as Defendant has shown that RFA responses were electronically served on Plaintiff on March 17, 2026 prior to the April 24, 2026 hearing.  The remainder of the Court’s April 24, 2026 minute order shall remain, including the sanctions award as Defendant did not request reconsideration of that portion of the order.

 

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event the parties submit on this tentative ruling, or a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records.

ON APRIL 24, 2026, THE COURT GRANTED PLAINTIFF’S UNOPPOSED MOTION FOR ORDER DEEMING REQUESTS FOR ADMISSIONS, SET TWO, ADMITTED AGAINST DEFENDANT GARY ENGLISH.  THE COURT NOW RECONSIDERS THAT PRIOR ORDER AND DENIES THE MOTION FOR ORDER DEEMING REQUESTS FOR ADMISSIONS, SET TWO, ADMITTED, AS DEFENDANT HAS NOW SHOWN THAT DISCOVERY RESPONSES WERE ELECTRONICALLY SERVED ON PLAINTIFF ON MARCH 17, 2026, PRIOR TO THE APRIL 24, 2026 HEARING.  THE REMAINDER OF THE COURT’S APRIL 24, 2026 MINUTE ORDER SHALL REMAIN. 

 

A FINAL STATUS CONFERENCE IS SET FOR JANUARY 21, 2027 AT 10:00 A.M. IN PERSON WITH TRIAL COUNSEL.

 

OSC RE FILING TRIAL BINDERS JANUARY 14, 2027 (NON-APPEARANCE)

 

COURT ISSUES A TRIAL PREPARATION ORDER, ALL PARTIES ARE ORDERED TO COMPLY WITH THE TRIAL ORDER INCORPORATED IN THE COURT’S DOCKET.

 

JURY TRIAL IS SET FOR JANUARY 25, 2027 AT 10:30 A.M.

 

DEFENDANT TO PROVIDE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.


Case Number: 24NNCV00806    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

motionS TO COMPEL FURTHER RESPONSES

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 24NNCV00806

 

MP:     Plaintiffs Debra Biane and Gerald Biane

RP:      Defendant Universal City Studios, LLC

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Debra Biane, Gerald Biane, Josh Taylorson, and Sami-Joh Goldberg (collectively “Plaintiffs”) allege that, on April 7, 2022, they were visitors of Universal City Studios LLC’s (“Defendant”) amusement park.  Plaintiffs allege that a malfunction in the “Harry Potter and the Forbidden Journey” ride caused the ride to stall, trapping Plaintiffs for approximately one hour.  Plaintiffs allege they sustained serious injury due to being trapped on the ride.

 

The Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”), filed February 23, 2026, alleges: (1) Premises Liability; (2) Negligence; (3) Common Carrier Liability; (4) Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress; and (5) Loss of Consortium. 

 

On April 3, 2026, Plaintiffs Sami-Joh Goldberg and Josh Taylorson dismissed the complaint with prejudice.  As such, the remaining Plaintiffs are Debra Biane and Gerald Biane.

 

MOTIONS ON CALENDAR:

 

There are four discovery motions on calendar.  On May 12, 2026, Plaintiffs Debra Biane and Gerald Biane each filed motions to compel Defendant’s further responses to: (1) Special Interrogatories, set two (“SROG”); and (2) Requests for Production of Documents, set two (“RPD”).  On August 28, 2026, Defendant filed opposition.  On September 3, 2026, Plaintiffs filed replies.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

A.     Motion to Compel Further Responses to Interrogatories

 

A motion to compel further interrogatory responses may be brought based on: (1) answers that are evasive or incomplete, (2)¿an unwarranted or insufficiently specific exercise of an option to produce documents in lieu of a substantive response, or (3) unmerited or overly generalized objections.  (C.C.P. §¿2030.300(a).)   The motion must be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration.  (C.C.P. § 2030.300(b)(1).)  The motion must be made within 45 days of service of the verified response or supplemental verified response, or on/before any specific late date to which the parties have agreed in writing.  (C.C.P. § 2030.300(c).) 

 

The responding party has the burden of justifying the objections thereto. (Coy v. Sup. Ct. (1962) 58 Cal.2d 210, 220-21.)

 

B.     Motion to Compel Further Responses to RPD

 

A motion to compel further RPD responses may be brought based on: (1) incomplete statements of compliance; (2) inadequate, evasive, or incomplete claims of inability to comply; or (3) unmerited or overly generalized objections.  (C.C.P. § 2031.310(a).) 

 

A motion to compel further production must set forth specific facts showing good cause justifying the discovery sought by the inspection demand and be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration. (C.C.P. § 2031.310(b)(1).)  “Good cause” is shown by “a disputed fact that is of consequence in the action and the discovery sought will tend in reason to prove or disprove that fact or lead to other evidence that will tend to prove or disprove the fact.”  (Digital Music News LLC v. Superior Court (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th 216, 224.)  The motion must be made within 45 days of service of the verified response or supplemental verified response, or on/before any specific late date to which the parties have agreed in writing.  (C.C.P. § 2031.310(c).) 

 

If the moving party has shown good cause for the requests for production, the burden is on the objecting party to justify the objections. (Kirkland v. Superior Court of Los Angeles County (2002) 95 Cal.App.4th 92, 98.) 

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     SROG

 

Biane Plaintiffs move to compel Defendant’s further responses to SROG Nos. 138-177.  The Court will consider the motions together as they involve essentially identical requests.

 

On July 7, 2026, the Court held an Informal Discovery Conference (“IDC”) and advised Defendant to provide supplemental discovery responses no later than July 24, 2026.  (July 7, 2026 Minute Order at p.1.) 

 

 

In opposition, Defendant represents that, following substitution of counsel and the IDC, it served omnibus supplemental responses to Biane Plaintiffs’ SROGs on July 28, 2026.  Copies of the supplemental responses are attached as Exhibit B to defense counsel Bianca Caro’s declarations. 

 

Biane Plaintiffs argue that the motions are not mooted by the supplemental responses because they are unverified, are not code-compliant, fail to identify witnesses, and improperly refer to C.C.P § 2030.230 placing the burden on Plaintiffs to sift through documents instead of receiving straightforward responses.

 

The motions to compel Defendant’s further responses to each of the Biane Plaintiffs’ SROGs are granted.  A review of the supplemental responses shows that they were not verified.  Thus, the motion is granted to the extent that Defendant will be ordered to provide verified, supplemental responses to the SROGs.  If Plaintiff still finds the discovery responses deficient, the parties are ordered to cooperate and engage in good faith meet and confer efforts telephonically or in person. 

 

B.     RPD

 

Biane Plaintiffs move to compel Defendant’s further responses to RPD Nos. 88-116. The Court will consider the two motions together.

 

For the same reasons discussed above, the Court grants the motions to compel Defendant’s further verified responses to the RPDs. 

 

C.     Sanctions

 

Biane Plaintiffs seek $2,560 in sanctions per SROG motion against Defendant and its counsel of record (= [2.9 hours for the motion] + [2.1 anticipated hours to review and reply to the opposition, and attend the hearing] at $500/hour, plus $60 filing fees).  (Schwar re SROG Motions, ¶¶17-19.) 

 

Biane Plaintiffs seek $2,760 in sanctions per RPD motion against Defendant and its counsel of record (= [3.3 hours for the motion] + [2.1 anticipated hours to review and reply to the opposition, and attend the hearing] at $500/hour, plus $60 filing fees).  (Schwar re RPD Motions, ¶¶17-19.) 

 

The Court will award sanctions in favor of Biane Plaintiffs for bringing these motions, as these motions and the IDC prompted Defendant to provide supplemental responses.  However, as represented by Biane Plaintiffs, the responses were unverified, such that Biane Plaintiffs were ultimately meritorious in their motions.  The requests for sanctions is granted in the amount of $2,060 per motion (= [4 hours per motion x $500/hour] + $60 filing fees), which the Court finds reasonable as the motions are essentially duplicative in form.

 

Biane Plaintiffs also seek to impose the motions against Defendant and its then-counsel of record, counsel of record Jaion Chung, Roya Fohrer, Bayan Salehi, Patrick Babajanian, and Kahana and Feld LLP, jointly and severally, as noticed in the motions.  Biane Plaintiffs argue that prior counsel cannot escape sanctions by withdrawing from the case.  (See e.g., Masimo Corp. v. The Vanderpool Law Firm, Inc. (2024) 101 Cal.App.5th 902, 909 [finding that the fact that firm exited representation shortly before discovery motion was filed did not insulate the firm from sanctions for its prior discovery misuse].)  The Court declines to enter sanctions against prior defense counsel.  Although Plaintiffs found Defendant’s initial responses to be unsatisfactory, the meet and confer records show the parties exchanged letters about the responses/objections.  Furthermore, the emails show that prior defense counsel, Patrick Babajanian, was amenable to resolving the issues informally, including by suggesting the IDC, which ultimately occurred and resulted in Defendant’s (unverified) supplemental responses.  (Babajanian Decl., Ex. G.)  Thus, sanctions will be imposed against Defendant only.

 

---

 

RULING:

 

In the event the parties submit on this tentative ruling, or a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Plaintiffs Debra Biane and Gerald Biane’s Motions to Compel Further Responses came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows: 

 

PLAINTIFFS DEBRA BIANE AND GERALD BIANE’S MOTIONS TO COMPEL DEFENDANT’S FURTHER RESPONSES TO SPECIAL INTERROGATORIES, SET TWO, AND RESPONSES TO REQEUSTS FOR PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS, SET TWO, ARE GRANTED.  RESPONSES ARE TO BE MADE WITHIN 30 DAYS.

 

DEFENDANT IS ORDERED TO PAY MONETARY SANCTIONS IN THE AMOUNT OF $4,120 TO PLAINTIFF DEBRA BIANE, BY AND THROUGH COUNSEL, WITHIN 30 DAYS OF THIS ORDER.

 

DEFENDANT IS ORDERED TO PAY MONETARY SANCTIONS IN THE AMOUNT OF $4,120 TO PLAINTIFF GERALD BIANE, BY AND THROUGH COUNSEL, WITHIN 30 DAYS OF THIS ORDER.

 

PLAINTIFF DEBRA BIANE TO PROVIDE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED. 


Case Number: 24NNCV02731    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

MOTION FOR SANCTIONS

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 24NNCV02731

 

MP:     Plaintiff Perla Ruiz

RP:      No opposition received

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

On July 5, 2024, Perla Ruiz (“Plaintiff”) filed the complaint against OI Chicks LLC (“Defendant”) for Enforcement Under the Private Attorneys General Act (“PAGA”).  Plaintiff brings this representative action, alleging that Defendant violated various wage and hour laws, including failure to provide employment records, pay overtime/double time, provide meal and rest breaks, pay minimum wages, keep accurate and provide itemized wage statements, pay reporting time, pay “split shift” premiums, timely pay wages during employment, timely pay wages upon termination, reimburse necessary business-related expenses and costs, and provide notice of paid sick time and accrual. 

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On May 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Further Monetary Sanctions, Issue Sanctions, and Evidentiary Sanctions.  The Court is not in receipt of an opposition brief.  The Court notes that, pursuant to C.R.C. Rule 8.54(c), a failure to oppose a motion may be deemed consent to its being granted.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

Under C.C.P. § 2023.030, the Court may impose issue sanctions ordering that designated facts be taken as established in the action in accordance with the claim of the party adversely affected by the misuse of the discovery process.  (C.C.P. § 2023.030(b).)  The Court may impose an evidence sanction by an order prohibiting any party engaging in the misuse of the discovery process from introducing designated matters in evidence.  (C.C.P. § 2023.030(c).)  Any motion for issue or evidentiary sanctions must be accompanied by a separate statement.  (CRC Rule 3.1345(a)(7).) 

 

Evidence or issue sanctions may be imposed only after parties violated discovery orders compelling further responses, except in exceptional circumstances, including where there was sufficiently egregious misconduct regarding a failure to respond to discovery, or a prior discovery order would be futile. (New Albertsons, Inc. v. Sup. Ct. (2008) 168 Cal.App.4th 1403, 1426.)  Two prerequisites for the imposition of non-monetary sanctions are: (1) there must be a failure to comply; and (2) the failure must be willful.  (Vallbona v. Springer (1996) 43 Cal.App.4th 1525, 1545.)  The party requesting sanctions under C.C.P. §§ 2023.030 and 2023.010(g) must establish that the other party has failed to comply or disobeyed a court order to provide discovery.  (C.C.P. § 2023.010(g); Miranda v. 21st Century Ins. Co. (2004) 117 Cal.App.4th 913, 929 [first requirement of failure to comply].)  To avoid sanctions, the burden of proving that a discovery violation was not willful is on the party on whom the discovery was served. (Cornwall v. Santa Monica Dairy Co. (1977) 66 Cal.App.3d 250, 252- 253.)

 

C.C.P. § 2023.030(a) states: “The court may impose a monetary sanction ordering that one engaging in the misuse of the discovery process, or any attorney advising that conduct, or both pay the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, incurred by anyone as a result of that conduct. The court may also impose this sanction on one unsuccessfully asserting that another has engaged in the misuse of the discovery process, or on any attorney who advised that assertion, or on both. If a monetary sanction is authorized by any provision of this title, the court shall impose that sanction unless it finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.”  Under California law, a discovery order cannot go further than is necessary to accomplish the purpose of discovery.  (Newland v. Superior Court (1995) 40 Cal. App. 4th 608, 613.)  The purpose of discovery sanctions is to prevent abuse of the discovery process and correct the problem presented.  (McGinty v. Superior Court (1994) 26 Cal. App. 4th 204, 210.) 

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

Plaintiff moves for: (1) further monetary sanctions in the amount of $5,157.70 against Defendant and its counsel of record; (2) issue sanctions; and (3) evidentiary sanctions, for Defendant’s violation of the Court’s October 31, 2025, November 14, 2025, and November 21, 2025 orders.

 

The following background is relevant:

 

·         On October 31, 2025, the Court granted Plaintiffs’ opposed Motion to Compel Defendant’s Answers to Form Interrogatories – Employment (set one) (“E-FROG”).  The Court noted that while Defendant represented it would serve code-complaint responses without objection prior to the hearing, the opposition and reply briefs showed that Defendant had not yet served responses.  No appearances were made at the hearing to indicate whether responses were in fact served prior to the hearing.  The Court granted the motion and ordered initial responses, without objection, within 30 days of the order.  The Court imposed $2,082.70 in sanctions against Defendant and its counsel of record, jointly and severally, to be payable within 30 days of the order.  (Mot., Ex. A.) 

 

·         On November 14, 2025, the Court granted Plaintiff’s opposed Motion to Compel Defendant’s Answers to Form Interrogatories – General (set one) (“FROG”).  Again, Defendant represented it would serve code-complaint responses prior to the hearing.  No appearances were made at the hearing to indicate whether responses were in fact served prior to the hearing.  The Court granted the motion and ordered initial responses, without objection, within 30 days of the order.  The Court imposed $1,582.70 in sanctions against Defendant and its counsel of record, jointly and severally, to be payable within 30 days of the order.  (Mot., Ex. B.)

 

·         On November 21, 2025, the Court granted Plaintiff’s opposed Motions to Compel Defendant’s initial responses to Special Interrogatories (“SROG”), set one, and Request for Production of Documents (“RPD”), set one; and denied Plaintiff’s opposed Motion to Deem the Requests for Admissions (“RFA”), set one, Admitted.  With respect to the RFA motion, the Court denied the motion because Defendant had shown that it served verified RFA responses on November 20, 2025 before the hearing.  With respect to the SROG and RPD motions, Defendant represented it would serve responses.  Although the parties appeared to the hearing, out of the abundance of caution, the Court granted the SROG and RPD motions, ordering Defendant to provide verified responses, without objection, within 30 days of the order.  The Court imposed $3,748.10 in sanctions against Defendant and its counsel of record, jointly and severally, to be payable within 30 days of the order.  The Court stated:

 

The Court notes that it should not take over a year to get responses to discovery which was agreed to be provided. Such actions unnecessarily delay cases and place a burden on the court system at a time when case loads are ever increasing and litigants have a challenging time obtaining timely resolution of disputes. The Court is sympathetic to the workloads which lawyers have, as apparently is plaintiff’s counsel who granted multiple extensions before resorting to motion practice. It was only the filing of the motion which resulted is a response, albeit one that was not code compliance and unverified.

           

            (Mot., Ex. C [Nov. 21, 2025 Minute Order at pp.8-9].) 

 

A.     Issue and Evidentiary Sanctions

 

Plaintiff seeks issue sanctions “prohibiting Defendant from contesting facts relating to Plaintiff’s employment, wages, hours, and payroll practices and/or that similar facts apply to the aggrieved employees that are the subject of Defendant’s unanswered discovery.”  (Mot. at 4:18-21.)  Additionally, Plaintiff seeks evidentiary sanctions “precluding Defendant from introducing evidence at motion practice or trial on subjects to Plaintiff’s outstanding discovery.”  (Id. at 4:21-23.)  Although a separate statement is not provided, Plaintiff lists the specific matters she seeks issue and evidentiary sanctions imposed upon on pages 9-11 of the motion. 

 

For issue sanctions, Plaintiff requests the following facts be deemed established for the purposes of this action that:

 

1. Plaintiff was employed by Defendant and suffered at least one labor code violation due to Defendant’s policies and practices, and thus has standing to pursue a representative PAGA claim.

 

2. Defendant failed to provide employment records in violation of Labor Code §§ 226, 432, and 1198.5 to Plaintiff and to each Aggrieved Employee as defined in the Complaint;

 

3-6. Defendant failed to (3) pay overtime and double time in violation of Labor Code § 510; (4) provide rest and meal periods in violation of Labor Code §§226.7, 512(a); (5) pay minimum wage in violation of Labor Code §§ 1182.2, 1194, 1197, 1197.1; and (6) keep accurate payroll records and provide itemized wage statements in violation of Labor Code §§ 226(a), 1174(d), 1198, as well as the applicable Wage Orders (“WOs”) during every pay period at issue to Plaintiff and to each Aggrieved Employee;

 

7-8. Defendant failed to pay (7) reporting time wages and (8) split shift wages, in violation of applicable WOs during every pay period at issue to Plaintiff and to each Aggrieved Employee;

 

9-12. Defendant failed to (9) pay all wages earned on time in violation of Labor Code § 204; (10) pay all wages earned upon discharge or resignation in violation of Labor Code §§ 201, 202, and 203; (11) reimburse necessary, business-related expenses in violation of Labor Code §§ 2800 and 2802; and (12) provide notice of paid sick time and accrual in violation of Labor Code § 24, during every pay period at issue to Plaintiff and to each Aggrieved Employee.

 

(Mot. at pp.9-10.)

 

For evidentiary sanctions, Plaintiff seeks:

 

a) Preclusion of any payroll, timekeeping, and policy evidence that seeks to establish compliance with the California Labor Code. Defendant should be precluded from introducing any documentary evidence, testimony, or argument in any motion practice or trial concerning payroll records, timekeeping data, meal- and rest-period practices, wage statements, or related policies, to the extent such evidence was required to be disclosed in response to Plaintiff’s FROG, SROG, and RPD.

 

b) Preclusion of any evidence supporting any of Defendant’s Affirmative Defenses. Defendant should be precluded from offering any documentary evidence or testimony in support of any affirmative defense that depends on information or documents withheld in violation of the Court’s discovery orders, including defenses relating to wage compliance, recordkeeping, or lawful employment practices.

 

c) Witness Preclusion. Defendant should be precluded from calling any witness—lay or expert—whose identity, knowledge, or anticipated testimony should have been disclosed in response to Plaintiff’s outstanding interrogatories or document requests.

 

(Mot. at pp.10-11.)

 

As of his May 6, 2026 declaration, Plaintiff’s counsel, Joseph C. Rocha, states that Defendant has not produced any objection-free, verified responses.  (Rocha Decl., ¶10.)  On January 13, 2026, Mr. Rocha emailed Defendant regarding responses and payment of sanctions, and defense counsel responded that it would comply “early next week.”  (Id., ¶11, Ex. D.)  On January 14, 2026, defense counsel Brendan Sapein responded that the client had indicated payment had been issued and that “we will be getting the production of documents to you this week, and the verified responses early next week.”  (Id., Ex. D.)  On January 20, 2026, Mr. Rocha emailed defense counsel for an update regarding production and payment, and Mr. Sapien responded on January 26, 2026 that Plaintiff would have “everything by the end of the week” (or presumably January 30, 2026).  (Id., ¶12, Ex. D.)  On February 2, 2026, Mr. Rocha emailed defense counsel advising them Plaintiff would file a second motion to compel if the Court’s orders were not met by February 6, 2026.  (Id., ¶13, Ex. D.)  On February 9, 2026, defense counsel responded that they would have payment by tomorrow and “we will be getting you the documents and response by Thursday of this week.”  (Id., ¶14, Ex. D.)  On February 17, 2026, Mr. Rocha emailed defense counsel that his office received the sanctions payment and asked for updates on responses.  (Id., ¶15, Ex. D.)  On February 19, 2026, Mr. Rocha sent another email seeking discovery responses.  (Id.)  On February 23, 2026, Mr. Sapien responded that they would be “rolling out production to you by tomorrow.”  (Id.)   On February 25, 2026, Mr. Rocha sent an email seeking an update, but did not hear back.  (Id.) 

 

On September 1, 2026, Defendant filed a Substitution of Attorney form, stating that its then-attorney Brendan Sapein of O’Hagan Meyer substituted out of the case and Defendant is now being represented by Mr. Sapien of Rutan & Tucker, LLP.  However, Defendant did not file an opposition by August 28, 2026. 

 

In light of the repeated discovery violations and the numerous informal attempts by Plaintiff to resolve the discovery issues, the Court grants this motion in part.  As a result of the discovery violations, Defendant is precluded from introducing any evidence related to their affirmative defenses, except those already produced by Defendant in written responses or in document production or those which have been produced by the Plaintiff in discovery.  Likewise, Defendant is precluded from introducing any evidence (documentary, witness testimony, or arguments) in defense of Defendant’s alleged Labor Code and WO violations, except those already produced by Defendant in written responses or in document production.  The Court declines to impose the issue and evidentiary sanctions sought by Plaintiff as such would be tantamount to terminating sanctions which is disfavored prior to imposition of escalating sanctions.

 

 

B.     Monetary Sanctions

 

Although the Court previously ordered sanctions, Plaintiff seeks an additional $5,157.70 in monetary sanctions against Defendant and its counsel, O’Hagan Meyer, jointly and severally.  This accounts for five hours Plaintiff’s counsel Joseph C. Rocha spent on pursuing this matter and drafting the motion, two anticipated hours to draft a reply and attend the hearing at $725/hour, and $82.70 in filing fees.  (Rocha Decl., ¶16.) 

 

Mr. Rocha states that Defendant has made a single late payment of $3,748.10 in response to the Court’s prior orders, such that $3,665.40 in past sanctions is still due.  (Rocha Decl., ¶10.)  He seeks a total of $8,823.40 in sanctions for the $5,157.70 he is currently requesting and the $3,665.40 in past-due sanctions.  (Id., ¶17.)

 

With respect to the remaining $3,665.40 in past-due sanctions, the request is denied.  Plaintiff  may enforce the orders that imposed monetary sanctions through the execution of judgment laws.  (Newland v. Superior Court (1995) 40 Cal. App. 4th 608, 615 [noting that many attorneys seem to be unaware that monetary sanction orders are enforceable through the execution of judgment laws].)  Orders imposing monetary sanctions have the force and effect of a money judgment, and are immediately enforceable through execution.  (Id.)  The Court will not reimpose those sanctions already entered and due. 

 

With respect to the additional $5,157.70 monetary sanctions request, the Court will award $3,625 for the time spent on this motion (= 5 hours at $725/hour), plus $82.70 in filing fees, for a total of $3,707.70.  The Court declines to award anticipated fees for the reply and attending the hearing as the motion is unopposed. 

 

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event the parties submit on this tentative ruling, or a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Plaintiff Perla Ruiz’s Motion for Sanctions came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows: 

 

PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR SANCTIONS IS GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART.  THE COURT GRANTS THE MOTION IN PART AND WILL IMPOSE EVIDENTIARY SANCTIONS AGAINST DEFENDANT SUCH THAT DEFENDANT SHALL BE:

 

Defendant IS precluded from introducing any documentary evidence, testimony, or argument in any motion practice or trial concerning payroll records, timekeeping data, meal- and rest-period practices, wage statements, or related policies, to the extent such evidence was required to be disclosed in response to Plaintiff’s FROG, SROG, and RPD.

 

Regarding Preclusion of any evidence supporting any of Defendant’s Affirmative Defenses: Defendant IS precluded from offering any documentary evidence or testimony in support of any affirmative defense that depends on information or documents withheld in violation of the Court’s discovery orders, including defenses relating to wage compliance, recordkeeping, or lawful employment practices.

 

Regarding Witness Preclusion: Defendant IS precluded from calling any LAY OR EXPERT witness whose identity, knowledge, or anticipated testimony should have been disclosed in response to Plaintiff’s outstanding interrogatories or document requests.

 

THE MOTION IS DENIED IN PART WITH RESPECT TO ISSUE SANCTIONS. 

 

THE MOTION IS GRANTED IN PART WITH RESPECT TO MONETARY SANCTIONS.   DEFENDANT AND ITS COUNSEL OF RECORD, JOINTLY AND SEVERALLY, ARE ORDERED TO PAY MONETARY SANCTIONS IN THE AMOUNT OF $3,707.70 TO PLAINTIFF, BY AND THROUGH COUNSEL, WITHIN 30 DAYS OF THIS ORDER.

 

PLAINTIFF TO PROVIDE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.


Case Number: 24NNCV06367    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

MOTION FOR TERMINATING SANCTIONS

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 24NNCV06367

 

MP:     Defendant Ashot Sargsyan

RP:      No opposition received

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Garnik Sahakian (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on August 18, 2023, he was involved in a motor vehicle collision with Ashot Sargsyan (“Defendant”), causing Plaintiff to suffer injuries. 

 

The complaint, filed December 6, 2024, alleges: (1) Motor Vehicle Negligence; and (2) General Negligence.

 

MOTIONS ON CALENDAR:

 

On May 18, 2026, Defendant filed a Motion for Terminating Sanctions and Monetary Sanctions.  The Court is not in receipt of an opposition brief.  The Court notes that, pursuant to C.R.C. Rule 8.54(c), a failure to oppose a motion may be deemed consent to its being granted. 

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

C.C.P. § 2023.030 permits the Court to impose terminating sanctions for discovery misuses, which are defined by C.C.P. § 2023.010 to include the failure to respond to an authorized method of discovery and the failure to comply with a Court discovery order. 

 

The Court weighs the following factors when considering the present motion: (1) defendants’ conduct, indicating whether their actions were willful; (2) the detriment to the party seeking discovery; and (3) the number of formal and informal unsuccessful attempts to obtain discovery.  (Lang v. Hochman (2000) 77 Cal.App.4th 1225, 1246.)  Ultimate discovery sanctions are justified where there is a willful discovery order violation, a history of abuse, and evidence showing that less severe sanctions would not produce compliance with discovery rules.  (Van Sickle v. Gilbert (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 1495, 1516.)

 

RELEVANT BACKGROUND:

 

On November 12, 2025, Defendant filed two motions to compel Plaintiff’s initial responses for: (1) Form Interrogatories (“FROG”), set one and Special Interrogatories (“SROG”), set one; and (2) Request for Production of Documents (“RPD”), set one.  The motions were served on Plaintiff’s then-counsel on November 12, 2025. The Order Granting Attorney’s Motion to be Relieved as Counsel indicated that a hearing on the motions to compel was scheduled for February 27, 2026. 

 

On November 14, 2025, the Court granted Plaintiff’s then-counsel’s motion to be relieved as counsel.  On December 2, 2025, Plaintiff’s then-counsel filed a Proof of Service – Civil, showing that the Order Granting Attorney’s Motion to be Relieved as Counsel was served by mail on Plaintiff at SBCSD High Desert Jail on December 2, 2025, such that Plaintiff was on notice of the February 27, 2026 hearing.  Plaintiff is currently a self-represented litigant. 

 

On February 27, 2026, the Court granted Defendant’s motions to compel Plaintiff’s initial responses to the FROG/SROG and RPD, ordering responses within 30 days of notice of the order.  The Court also imposed $620 in sanctions, payable within 30 days of the order.  The Court ordered Defendant to file a proof of service indicating that Defendant served Plaintiff with the order, as Plaintiff appeared to be incarcerated. 

 

On March 5, 2026, Defendant filed a Notice of Ruling of the Court’s February 27, 2026 order, showing that Defendant served Plaintiff by mail at the High Desert Detention Center. 

 

ANALYSIS:

 

A.     Terminating Sanctions

 

On February 27, 2026, the Court granted Defendant’s motion to compel discovery responses.  Plaintiff was ordered to provide responses within 30 days of notice of the Court’s order.  Defendant mailed notice of the order on March 5, 2026.   On April 7, 2026, defense counsel Nageen C. Jalali states that Defendant attempted to contact Plaintiff by sending him a letter, requesting responses.  (Jalali Decl., ¶4, Ex. C.)  Defense counsel states that while they received some calls from someone they can only assume was Plaintiff calling them from prison, Plaintiff was unable to speak long enough for defense counsel to talk to him and defense counsel was unable to contact Plaintiff except by letter.  (Mot. at p.6.)  Defendant asserts that from what little Plaintiff was able to provide, he stated that he did not know what was going on and directed Defendant to speak with his lawyer.  (Id.)  However, as noted above, Plaintiff’s counsel withdrew from the case and it does not appear that Plaintiff has retained new counsel. 

 

Defendant contends that as of the date of filing the motion on May 18, 2026, Plaintiff has not yet provided responses or paid the monetary sanctions. 

 

Based on Plaintiff’s failure to comply with the Court’s order, lack of opposition to the motion, and failure to provide responses despite Defendant’s attempts to contact Plaintiff, it appears that Plaintiff has abandoned this case.  In light of Plaintiff’s conduct, there is no reason to believe that any lesser issue/evidentiary sanctions will force him to comply with his discovery obligations.  Accordingly, the motion for terminating sanctions is granted. 

 

B.     Monetary Sanctions

 

Under California law, a discovery order cannot go further than is necessary to accomplish the purpose of discovery.  (Newland v. Superior Court (1995) 40 Cal. App. 4th 608, 613.)  The purpose of discovery sanctions is to prevent abuse of the discovery process and correct the problem presented.  (McGinty v. Superior Court (1994) 26 Cal. App. 4th 204, 210.)

 

Defendant seeks $1,350 for having to file this motion (= [2.5 hours on the motion] + [3 anticipated hours to review and reply to the opposition and attend the hearing] at $220/hour).  (Jalali Decl., ¶9.) 

 

There is no reason to grant monetary sanctions in addition to terminating sanctions, since such an award would not advance the purpose of discovery sanctions any further than the termination of the case.  Therefore, the request for additional monetary sanctions is denied.

 

The Court notes that the granting of terminating sanctions is justified as there are no lesser sanctions which have been successful; however, given that Plaintiff is incarcerated and his counsel withdrew, the Court believes that dismissing the complaint without prejudice versus with prejudice is in the interest of justice.

 

--- 

 

RULING:

Case Number: 25NNCV00077    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

MOTION FOR LEAVE TO WITHDRAW DEEMED ADMISSIONS

MOTION FOR JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV00077

 

(1) Motion for Leave to Withdraw Deemed Admissions

MP:     Defendant Luis Carmona

RP:      Plaintiff Headway Capital, LLC

 

(2) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings

MP:     Plaintiff Headway Capital, LLC

RP:      Defendant Luis Carmona

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS AND RELEVANT BACKGROUND:

 

Headway Capital, LLC (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on February 3, 2023, it entered into a written Business Use Line of Credit Agreement (“Agreement”) with Forward Inglewood, Inc. (“Forward”) and Luis Carmona (“Carmona”) (collectively, “Defendants”), wherein Carmona personally guaranteed the loan.  Plaintiff alleges that within the last four years, Defendants defaulted under the Agreement’s terms and failed to make payment thereunder, thereby breaching the Agreement. Plaintiff seeks $81,638.62 in damages.

 

The Complaint, filed January 6, 2025, alleges a single cause of action for Breach of Contract. 

 

On February 24, 2025, Carmona (a self-represented litigant) answered.  On January 9, 2026, the Court granted Plaintiff’s unopposed motion for an order deeming RFAs admitted against Carmona and ordered Carmona to pay $60 in sanctions within 30 days of the order.   

 

On April 23, 2026, Forward’s default was entered. 

 

MOTIONS ON CALENDAR:

 

On July 9, 2026, Carmona filed a Motion for Leave to Withdraw Deemed Admissions and to Vacate or Set Aside January 9, 2026 Order.  On August 4, 2026, Plaintiff filed an opposition.  On September 4, 2026, Carmona filed an untimely reply (due by September 3, 2026).

 

On July 15, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings (“MJOP”).  On August 31, 2026, Carmona filed an untimely opposition (due by August 28, 2026).  (The Court notes that on August 31, 2026, Carmona filed a Substitution of Attorney form, stating that he was formerly a self-represented litigant and has now retained counsel.)    

 

RELEVANT BACKGROUND:

 

On August 15, 2025, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Order Deeming the RFA Admitted against Carmona.  The proof of service indicates that the RFA motion was served via mail on “Forward Inglewood, Inc., 208 La Brea Ave, Inglewood CA 90301” and “Luis Carmona, 330 Arden Ave Ste 110, Glendale CA 91203.” 

 

On January 9, 2026, the Court granted Plaintiff’s unopposed Motion to Deem the RFAs Admitted against Carmona.  The Court ordered Carmon to pay $60 in monetary sanctions to within 30 days of this order.  

 

On January 15, 2026, Plaintiff’s Notice of Ruling shows that it was served on “Forward Inglewood, Inc. Unk” at 208 S. La Brea Ave., Inglewood, CA 90301.  On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Notice of Order regarding the January 9, 2026 Order, stating that it was served on Carmona at 330 Arden Ave, #110, Glendale CA 91203. 

 

On July 31, 2026, Plaintiff’s MJOP initially came for hearing.  The Court continued the hearing to September 11, 2026 because: (1) a “Notice of Continued Hearing” was mailed on July 14, 2026 to “Luis Carmona c/o Laura Portillo, Esq. / PORTILLO RONK LEGAL TEAM” at 5176 Corsa Ave, Ste. 207 Westlake Village, CA 91362” and Carmona at the Arden address, but it did not appear that the MJOP papers themselves were served on Carmona; and (2) judicial economy would be promoted by considering Carmona’s Motion to Withdraw Deemed Admissions concurrently with Plaintiff’s MJOP. 

 

The Court notes that though Portillo Ronk Legal Team was served with the Notice of Continued Hearing (filed July 14, 2026) and is identified as “Counsel for Defendant Luis Carmona” for Carmona’s July 9, 2026 Motion to Withdraw Deemed Admissions, there is no substitution of attorney form filed indicating that Carmona was represented by legal counsel at that time.

 

On August 31, 2026, Carmona filed a Substitution of Attorney form stating that he was formerly a self-represented litigant and is now being represented by attorney Laura Portillo. 

 

MOTION TO WITHDRAW DEEMED ADMISSIONS ANALYSIS:

 

A.     Legal Standard

 

C.C.P. § states:

 

(a) A party may withdraw or amend an admission made in response to a request for admission only on leave of court granted after notice to all parties.

 

(b) The court may permit withdrawal or amendment of an admission only if it determines that the admission was the result of mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect, and that the party who obtained the admission will not be substantially prejudiced in maintaining that party's action or defense on the merits.

 

(c) The court may impose conditions on the granting of the motion that are just, including, but not limited to, the following:

 

(1) An order that the party who obtained the admission be permitted to pursue additional discovery related to the matter involved in the withdrawn or amended admission.

 

(2) An order that the costs of any additional discovery be borne in whole or in part by the party withdrawing or amending the admission.

 

(C.C.P. § 2033.300; Wilcox v. Birtwhistle (1999) 21 C4th 973, 979-980 [finding that relief may be granted even if no responses were served]; Weil & Brown, The Rutter Guide, Cal. Prac. Guide Civ. Pro. Before Trial (June 2026 Update) Ch. 8G-8, § 8:1386b [“Even though CCP § 2033.300 refers only to withdrawal or amendment of an admission, this includes admissions deemed admitted by the court under CCP § 2033.280(b) for failure to respond.”].)

 

The discretionary prong of C.C.P. § 473(b) states:

 

The court may, upon any terms as may be just, relieve a party or his or her legal representative from a judgment, dismissal, order, or other proceeding taken against him or her through his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. Application for this relief shall be accompanied by a copy of the answer or other pleading proposed to be filed therein, otherwise the application shall not be granted, and shall be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the judgment, dismissal, order, or proceeding was taken.

 

(C.C.P. § 473(b).) 

 

B.     Discussion

 

Carmona moves to vacate the Court’s January 9, 2026 order deeming the RFAs admitted, withdraw the deemed admissions, permit Carmona to serve verified RFA responses, and continue or deny Plaintiff’s MJOP as it relies on the deemed admissions.  A copy of the proposed RFA responses is attached as Exhibit A to the motion.  (Carmona Decl., ¶10, Ex. A.)

 

In support of the motion, Carmona provides his declaration.  Carmona states he did not receive actual notice of Plaintiff’s RFA motion in time to oppose or serve responses before the hearing, he did not intentionally ignore the motion, and he did not intend to admit liability or concede issues raised by the RFAs.  (Carmona Decl., ¶3.)  He states that during the relevant time period, his mailing/service address was: 330 Arden Ave #110, Glendale CA 91203.  (Id., ¶4.)  He states he did not receive the RFA motion at that address nor the January 15, 2026 Notice of Ruling.  (Id., ¶¶5-6.)  The Notice of Ruling’s proof of service states that “Forward Inglewood, Inc. Unk” was served but does not identify Carmona individually as a person served.  (Id., ¶6.)  He states that he first learned of the deemed admission on July 6, 2026 when he received the MJOP via mail.  (Id., ¶7.)  After he learned of the order and Plaintiff’s attempt to use the deemed admissions in the MJOP, he promptly sought legal assistance and asked counsel to seek relief from the deemed admissions.  (Id., ¶8.)  He disputes Plaintiff’s claims and contends that Plaintiff should not obtain judgment based on admissions due to lack of notice and service problems.  (Id., ¶9.)

 

Carmona argues that the RFAs were deemed admitted as a result of mistake, inadvertence, surprise, and excusable neglect because he did not receive actual notice at his correct address, as evidenced by Plaintiff’s inconsistent service records.   He relies on Plaintiff’s January 15, 2026 Notice of Ruling of the Court’s January 9, 2026 Order, which was served on Forward only, which differed from Plaintiff’s purported service of the MJOP to Carmona’s Arden address.  He argues that these inconsistencies in Plaintiff’s service to the correct address support granting his motion based on surprise and excusable neglect.

 

First, Carmona must establish that the admissions were the result of mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect.

 

The Court finds that Carmona has met this burden.  Carmona affirms that his address was the Arden address and Plaintiffs’ proof of service shows that the RFA motion was served to this address.  However, Carmona states he did not receive the RFA motion at his address, and only learned about the RFA Motion when he received the Notice of Ruling on July 6, 2026 by mail.  (Carmona Decl., ¶¶4-5, 7.)  The Court will accept Carmona’s representation made under the penalty of perjury that he did not receive notice of the RFA motion.  As he claims he did not receive the RFA motion, he has established that the omissions were the result of mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect for his failure to oppose or prepare RFA responses prior to the hearing.

 

Second, the Court must determine whether Plaintiff (the party who obtained the admission) will not be substantially prejudiced in maintaining its action on the merits. 

 

Carmona argues that Plaintiff will not suffer substantial prejudice because this is a straightforward collections case, such that there is no risk of lost evidence, unavailability of witnesses, etc. and denying Carmona relief would result in a windfall to Plaintiff.  In opposition, Plaintiff argues that it would suffer prejudice because it detrimentally relied on the Court’s January 9, 2026 Order, forewent pursuing additional discovery, and drafted the MJOP.  Plaintiff contends that it was actively pursuing judgment and that granting this motion would reopen discovery after Carmona’s nearly year-long delay. 

 

However, the Court does not find that Plaintiff’s claim of prejudice to be so great as to warrant denying the motion.  While granting Carmona’s requested relief will result in an inconvenience and delay to Plaintiff, the Court recognizes that the law strongly favors trial and disposition on the merits.”  (See Henderson v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co. (2010) 187 Cal.App.4th 215, 230.) 

 

As such, Carmona’s Motion for Leave to Withdraw Deemed Admissions and to Vacate or Set Aside January 9, 2026 Order is granted.  The deemed admissions against Carmona entered on January 9, 2026 shall be withdrawn.   

 

MOTION FOR JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     Legal Standard

 

A plaintiff may move for judgment on the pleadings on the ground that: (1) the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause or causes of action against the defendant and (2) the answer does not state facts sufficient to constitute a defense to the complaint.  (C.C.P. § 438(c)(1)(A).)  The grounds for the motion shall appear on the face of the challenged pleading or from any matter of which the Court is required to take judicial notice. (C.C.P. § 438(d).)

 

“Any matter admitted in response to a request for admission is conclusively established against the party making the admission for purposes of the pending action, unless the court permits a withdrawal or amendment of the admission under section 2033.300. (§ 2033.410, subd. (a).)”  (New Albertsons, Inc. v. Superior Court (2008) 168 Cal.App.4th 1403, 1418.) 

 

B.     Meet and Confer

 

C.C.P. § 439(a) requires that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the motion for judgment on the pleadings. Upon review, the Court finds the meet and confer requirements were met.  (Marquez Decl., ¶¶10-11.)      

 

C.     Discussion

 

Plaintiff seeks judgment on the pleading, arguing: (1) Carmona’s answer does not controvert Plaintiff’s allegations in the Complaint, (2) the Requests for Admissions (“RFAs”) were admitted against Carmona (Mot., Ex. 1 [RFAs], Ex. 2 [January 9, 2026 Order]), and (3) the Complaint alleges sufficient facts against Defendant.

 

In light of the ruling on Carmona’s Motion for Leave to Withdraw Deemed Admissions and to Vacate or Set Aside January 9, 2026 Order, the MJOP is denied as the RFAs are no longer deemed admitted. 

 

As the deemed admissions were the sole basis for Plaintiff’s MJOP, the MJOP is denied. 

 

--- 

 

RULING:

ORDER 

 

Defendant Luis Carmona’s Motion for Leave to Withdraw Deemed Admissions and Plaintiff Headway Capital, LLC’s Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026 with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows: 

 

DEFENDANT CARMONA’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO WITHDRAW DEEMED ADMISSIONS AND TO VACATE OR SET ASIDE THE JANUARY 9, 2026 ORDER IS GRANTED. 

 

PLAINTIFF HEADWAY CAPITAL, LLC’S Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings IS DENIED.
