DEMURRER

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV00854

 

MP:     Defendant City of Los Angeles

RP:      No opposition filed, but it appears Plaintiff may have served a copy on City  

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Derrick Tucker (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on February 16, 2024, he rented an electric scooter from Defendant Neutron Holdings, Inc dba Lime (“Lime”) and was riding it between 11829 Victory Blvd. and 11835 Victory Blvd.  Plaintiff alleges that Defendants Adrian De La Hoya Jr. (“Hoya”) and Victory Villas LLC (“VVL”), and Espinoza Apiaries (“EA”) improperly placed wooden beams and/or similar objects strapped to a parked vehicle in a poorly lit/illuminated area.  Plaintiff alleges that Hoya and VVL negligently owned, maintained, managed, and operated the premises.  Plaintiff alleges that Defendants City of Los Angeles (“City”) owned the public property on which the dangerous condition existed and that its employees created the condition.

 

The Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”), filed March 26, 2026, alleges: (1) General Negligence; (2) Premises Liability; and (3) Products Liability. 

 

On June 26, 2026, Plaintiff dismissed without prejudice California Department of Transportation, State of California, Neutron Holdings, Inc. dba Lime, and Victory Villas LLC.

 

RELEVANT BACKGROUND AND MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 24, 2026, City filed a demurrer to the SAC.  The Court is not in receipt of an opposition brief.  The Court notes that, pursuant to C.R.C. Rule 8.54(c), a failure to oppose a motion may be deemed consent to its being granted.  On September 3, 2026, City filed a substantive reply addressing Plaintiff’s opposition arguments.

 

ANALYSIS:

 

City demurs to the Second Cause of Action for Premises Liability as to Count 3 – Dangerous Condition of Public Property on the grounds that it fails to allege sufficient facts because: (1) the SAC fails to allege any City-owned property; and (2) City is statutorily immune under Government Code, § 818.2 for any injury caused by its alleged failure to enforce parking laws and obstruction ordinances. 

 

Plaintiff’s opposition was due by August 28, 2026.  Based on the Court’s review of the documents filed in this action, Plaintiff did not file an opposition.  However, City reply brief addresses the substantive arguments in Plaintiff’s opposition.  Thus, it appears that Plaintiff may have served but did not file a copy of the opposition. 

 

Thus, the Court will continue the hearing on the demurrer so that Plaintiff may file the opposition.  No further briefing will be permitted.

Case Number: 25NNCV06491    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

MOTION FOR ATTORNEY’s FEES, COSTS, and EXPENSES

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV06491

 

MP:     Plaintiff Arman Khachatryan

RP:      Defendant General Motors LLC

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Arman Khachatryan (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on September 25, 2024, he leased a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq, which was accompanied by express and implied warranties from General Motors LLC (“Defendant”).  Plaintiff asserts that the vehicle was delivered with serious defects and nonconformities to the warranty, including defective electrical and mechanical components.  Plaintiff claims that despite a reasonable number of repair attempts, Defendant was unable to conform the vehicle to applicable warranties. 

 

The Complaint, filed September 15, 2025, alleges causes of action for: (1) Breach of Express Warranty Obligations Under Song-Beverly Act; and (2) Breach of Implied Warranty Obligations Under Song-Beverly Act.

 

On May 22, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Notice of Conditional Settlement of Entire Case. 

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On May 28, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Attorney’s Fees, Costs, and Expenses.  On August 28, 2026, Defendant filed an opposition.  On September 1, 2026, Plaintiff filed two copies of the reply brief—one at 11:41 a.m. and the other at 11:59 a.m.  The Court will consider the later-filed reply.

 

An OSC re: Dismissal (Settlement) is concurrently scheduled this date.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

A prevailing party in an action under the Song-Beverly Act may be entitled to reasonable attorney's fees. (Civ. Code § 1794(d); see also C.C.P. § 1032(a)(4).) The calculation of attorney's fees under the Song-Beverly Act is based on the lodestar method, which multiplies the number of hours reasonably expended by a reasonable hourly rate. (Graciano v. Robinson Ford Sales (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 140, 154; Robertson v. Fleetwood Travel Trailers of California, Inc. (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 785, 817-819.) Nonetheless, the prevailing party should not receive a "windfall" through an award of reasonable attorney's fees. (Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1132.) Thus, a prevailing buyer under the Song-Beverly Act has the burden of "showing that the fees incurred were 'allowable,' were 'reasonably necessary to the conduct of the litigation,' and were 'reasonable in amount.’" (Levy v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc. (1992) 4 Cal.App.4th 807, 816.)

 

Once an attorney has presented evidence of their actual time spent and hourly rate charged, the time and hourly rate are presumed to be reasonable, unless “special circumstances” render the award unjust. (Serrano v. Unruh (1982) 32 Cal.3d 621, 639.) An award of attorney fees may be based on counsel's declarations, without production of detailed time records. (Raining Data Corp. v. Barrenechea (2009) 175 Cal.App.4th 1363, 1375.) The verified time statements of attorneys, as officers of the court, are entitled to credence in the absence of a clear indication the records are erroneous. (Horsford v. Board of Trustees of California State University (2005) 132 Cal.App.4th 359, 396.)

 

The California Supreme Court has opined that an attorney should not receive a windfall relative to statutes which award attorney’s fees.  As such, “plaintiffs' counsel are not permitted to take contractual fees in addition to statutory fees: If the contingency fee is larger than the statutory fee award, counsel is permitted to accept that fee, with a setoff for statutory fees received. If the contingency fee is smaller than the statutory fee, counsel must reimburse the plaintiff from the statutory award for any amounts already paid by the client pursuant to the contingency contract.” (Horsford v. Board of Trustees of California State University (2005) 132 Cal.App.4th 359, 401 [citing Flannery v. Prentice (2001) 26 Cal.4th 572, 577].)

 

ANALYSIS:

 

Plaintiff moves for attorney’s fees and costs in the amount of $23,842.50 in attorney’s fees, $3,000 in anticipated fees for this motion, a 0.5 lodestar multiplier for $11,921.25, and costs of $551.67, for a total of $39,315.42.

 

A.     Prevailing Party and Basis for Attorney’s Fees

 

In the moving papers, Plaintiff does not address his entitlement to fees.  At most, he argues that pursuant to the terms of a 998 Offer to Compromise, Plaintiff is entitled to file this motion and that Defendant agreed Plaintiff is the prevailing party for the purposes of an attorney’s fees’ motion, citing Plaintiff’s counsel Claude Manookian’s declaration at paragraph 28.  (See Mot. at 3:21-28.)  A review of Mr. Manookian’s declaration shows that it ends at paragraph 24 and does not discuss the 998 Offer.  

 

In Defendant’s opposition, defense counsel Ryan Kay states that after eight months of litigation, the parties reached a settlement preceding mediation in “February 2024,” and Plaintiff executed a settlement agreement on March 6, 2026.  (Kay Decl., ¶9.) 

 

Although a copy of the settlement agreement is not attached, it does not appear that Defendant opposes Plaintiff’s characterization as the prevailing party for the purposes of this motion, nor does it argue that fees are not permitted on contractual and/or statutory grounds.

 

However, for completeness of the record, the Court will continue the hearing and order Plaintiff to file a copy of the 998 Offer and/or executed settlement agreement, showing that the parties agreed that Plaintiff may seek attorney’s fees by motion and that Plaintiff is deemed the prevailing party for the purposes of a motion for attorney’s fees. 

 

B.     Amount of Reasonable Attorney’s Fees

 

Plaintiff seeks $23,842.50 in attorney’s fees for fees incurred and an additional $3,000 for anticipated fees for this motion. 

 

Plaintiff’s counsel Claude Manookian provides the firm’s billing records.  (Manookian Decl., ¶8, Ex. A.)  Mr. Manookian is the founder and managing partner of Manookian Law, APLC and bills at $800/hour.  (Id., ¶¶3-5.)  Senior associate, Artin Boghouzian (admitted 2021), bills at $325/hour. (Id., ¶10.) 

 

While the billing records seek a total of $23,842.50, the Court notes that the billing records include timekeepers “CM”, “AB”, “MS”, and “RM”.  While CM and AB are presumably Claude Manookian and Artin Boghouzian, respectively, the Court is unaware of the identity and roles of MS and RM (who each bill at $175/hour). 

 

Furthermore, the motion’s memorandum of points and authorities, Mr. Manookian’s declaration, and the billing records do not provide the total amount of hours each timekeeper spent, such that the Court cannot conduct a lodestar analysis. 

 

Thus, the Court continues the hearing on this motion so that Plaintiff may: (1) identify the other timekeepers in the billing records and justify their hourly rates and time spent on this action; and (2) provide the total hours each timekeeper spent so that the Court can conduct a lodestar analysis. 

 

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Plaintiff Arman Khachatryan’s Motion for Attorney’s Fees, Costs, and Expenses came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows:  

 

THE MOTION FOR ATTORNEY’S FEES AND COSTS IS CONTINUED TO OCTOBER 2, 2026 at 9:00 a.m.   

 

PLAINTIFF IS ORDERED TO FILE AND SERVE A SUPPLEMENTAL BRIEF (NOT TO EXCEED FIVE PAGES) BY SEPTEMBER 18, 2026 REGARDING: (1) THE 998 OFFER AND/OR SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT; AND (2) THE ADDITIONAL TIMEKEEPERS AND THE TOTAL AMOUNT OF HOURS EACH TIMEKEEPER SPENT.  DEFENDANT MAY FILE AND SERVE A RESPONSIVE SUPPLEMENTAL BRIEF (NOT TO EXCEED FIVE PAGES) BY SEPTEMBER 28, 2026. 

 

THE COURT DISMISSES THIS MATTER WITHOUT PREJUDICE BUT SUBJECT TO THE COURT’S RETAINED JURISDICTION, INCLUDING THE RULING ON THE FEE MOTION, PURSUANT TO CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE §664.6.

 

Plaintiff TO GIVE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.


Case Number: 25NNCV07248    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

(CONTINUED FROM AUGUST 14, 2026)

MOTION TO QUASH SERVICE

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV07248

 

MP:     Defendant Purrfect Mechanical Services, Inc.

RP:      Plaintiff Emeka V. Peter

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Emeka V. Peter (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on December 9, 2024, he took his car to Purrfect Mechanical Services, Inc. (“Defendant”) and provided his own part for repair.  Plaintiff alleges Defendant charged Plaintiff $200 for the repair and took possession of his vehicle to fix the master brake system.  Although the repair was supposed to be completed the same day, Defendant falsely informed Plaintiff that the repair would not be finished because the person responsible for bleeding the brake system was unavailable.  After five days, Plaintiff returned, paid Defendant $100, and noticed that the repair had not been completed and that there was a crack in his windshield.  Upon return, Defendant refused to perform the windshield replacement or repair the coding system unless Plaintiff paid the remaining $100 balance.  Plaintiff alleges Defendant’s conduct, his windshield, the brake system, and coding system were left in a damaged and unsafe condition, depriving him of the use of his vehicle.

 

The Complaint, filed October 14, 2025, alleges: (1) Negligence; (2) Breach of Contract; (3) Breach of Warranty; (4) Property Damage; and (5) Loss of Use.

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On May 1, 2026, Defendant filed a Motion to Quash Service of the Complaint.  On May 27, 2026, Plaintiff (a self-represented litigant) filed an opposition.  On July 24, 2026, Defendant filed a reply.  On July 30, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Notice of Errata regarding Ada Peter’s declaration.  

 

The matter initially came for hearing on August 14, 2026.  Plaintiff requested, and the Court granted, an Evidentiary Hearing (Evidence Code, § 402) for September 11, 2026 at 1:45 p.m. 

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

C.C.P. § 418.10(a)(1) states: “A defendant, on or before the last day of his or her time to plead or within any further time that the court may for good cause allow, may serve and file a notice of motion” to “quash service of summons on the ground of lack of jurisdiction of the court over him or her.”

 

C.C.P. § 415.10 states in relevant part: 

 

A summons may be served by personal delivery of a copy of the summons and of the complaint to the person to be served. Service of a summons in this manner is deemed complete at the time of such delivery.

 

(C.C.P. § 415.10.)

 

REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE:

 

With the motion, Defendant requests judicial notice of Exhibits: (A) the Proof of Service of Hayk Mirimanyan dated October 13, 2025 in this action; (B) Proof of Service in Case No. 25VECV07298 on Hayk Mirimanyan dated October 22, 2025; and (C) Proof of Service in Case No. 25VECV07398 on Hayk Mirimanyan dated April 8, 2026.  The request is granted.  (Evid. Code, § 452(d).)

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     Proof of Service

 

On December 22, 2025, Plaintiff filed the Proof of Service of Summons, indicating that Defendant was personally served on October 22, 2025 at 4:30 by serving Hayk Mirimanyan at 4350 Whitsett Avenue, Studio City, CA 91604.  Service was effectuated by Ada Peter, who is not a registered California process server. 

 

B.     Discussion

 

Defendant moves to quash service of the summons and complaint.  

 

In support of the motion, Defendant provides Hayk Mirimanyan’s declaration.  Mr. Mirimanyan states that he has been Defendant’s agent since 2017 and is the principal officer.  (Mirimanyan Decl., ¶4.)  He believes that on the dates he was supposed to be in the shop and personally served with the legal papers, he was either in his home office or with business associates. (Id., ¶6.)  He states that on October 22, 2025, he was never at the business location at 4350 Whitsett Avenue and has never been served by any means with the summons and complaint in this action.  (Id., ¶7.)  He states he first became aware of the legal documents on April 8, 2026, when his manager Andy Kepenyan told him about the lawsuit; he then saw the documents on April 28, 2026 when he met with his attorney Donald M. Shirwo.  (Id., ¶9.)  He states that he spoke with his employees at the business location and no one received the summons and complaint documents.  (Id., ¶10.)

 

Mr. Kepenyan provides his declaration, stating that he is Defendant’s manager and regularly at the business location daily from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. except Saturday and Monday.  (Kepenyan Decl., ¶¶3-4.)  He states that he was at the business address on October 22, 2025 and that for all business hours of that day, Mr. Mirimanyan was not present at any time and he normally was not present at the location unless there was an emergency or something unusual.  (Id., ¶5.)  On “April 8, 2026,” Mr. Kepenyan states he was at the business location all day and that later in the afternoon, a woman parked her car in the driveway, walked up to the counter, and dropped a sealed envelope and left the business.  (Id., ¶6.)  He states he opened the sealed envelope and inside was the Case management Statement, and that he called Mr. Mirimanyan about the paperwork.  (Id., ¶7.)  When he was subsequently shown the legal documents by Mr. Shirwo, he states that no one delivered those documents to the business on October 13 or 22, 2025 and that the woman who dropped the sealed envelope on “April 7, 2026” was never on the business premises on October 13 or 22, 2025.  (Id., ¶8.)  (The Court notes that the Case Management Statement filed April 7, 2026 includes a proof of service showing that Ada Peters personally served the document on Hayk Mirimanyan on behalf of Defendant on April 7, 2026.) 

 

Defense counsel Darold M. Shirwo provides his declaration, stating that he is a regular customer of Defendant, an avid car collector, and regularly has one to two cars at Defendant’s shop such that he is at the premises at least two to three times a week.  (Shirwo Decl., ¶¶4-6.)  Mr. Shirwo states that he has spoken to all Defendant’s employees (Karlin Khachayryan, Andy “Kepentyan”, Alfredo Ortega, and Alex Contreras) who were working on October 13 and 22, 2025, and no one remembers a woman or anyone else delivering legal papers or a sealed envelope during business hours nor do they remember Mr. Mirimanyan being present at the shop those days.  (Id., ¶8.) 

 

In opposition, Plaintiff argues that Defendant does not deny that Mr. Mirimanyan is Defendant’s agent and that Defendant relies on self-serving declarations when a non-party, non-registered adult process server served Defendant. 

 

Plaintiff provides Ada Peter’s declaration, wherein she states that “[o]n or before” October 22, 2025, she personally went to Defendant’s business location for the purpose of serving legal documents.  (Ada Peter Decl., ¶3.)  She states she was instructed by Plaintiff to confirm the identity and take a picture of the person served, she personally observed and spoke with Mr. Mirimanyan, she personally delivered the summons and complaint on Mr. Mirimanyan, and she took a photograph of Mr. Mirimanyan depicting the individual who accepted service on Defendant’s behalf.  (Id., ¶¶4-9; Ex. A [Photographs].)  

 

In her corrected declaration, Ada Peter states that there was a typographical error in paragraph 3 of her prior declaration, such that the correct language should be: “On or after October 22, 2025, I personally went to the business location of Purrfect Mechanical Services, Inc., located at or near 4350 Whitsett Avenue, Studio City, California, for the purpose of serving legal documents in this case.”  (Corrected Ada Peter Decl., ¶3 [underline added].)  She states that all other statements in her prior declaration remain true and correct. (Id.) 

 

In reply, Defendant argues that Plaintiff’s evidence is based on perjury and amounts to deceit because Plaintiff’s photograph depicts a brown Oldsmobile Tornado on the left side of the photograph, which Defendant circles in its Reply Exhibit 2, showing a car that is owned by Mr. Shirwo that was not located at the premises on October 22, 2025.  Mr. Shirwo states that he purchased that car on January 2, 2026 and delivered the vehicle to Defendant between April 5 to April 8, 2026.   (Shriwo Reply Decl., ¶¶3-4, Ex. 2 [Circled Photograph]; Kepenyan Decl., ¶¶5-6.)  Thus, Defendant argues that Plaintiff’s submitted photograph and Ms. Peter’s declaration are acts of perjury. 

 

At this point, the Court cannot ascertain when the photograph was taken as there is no time stamp and Ada Peter does not state the exact date she took the photograph.  However, based on the evidence submitted by the parties, Mr. Mirimanyan and Mr. Kepenyan state that Mr. Mirimanyan was not on the premises on October 22, 2025 to personally accept service.  Furthermore, Defendant has provided a reasonable explanation that the photograph could not have been taken on October 22, 2025 and that it was likely taken on April 7 or 8, 2026 when Ada Peters delivered the Case Management Statement.  

 

The Court also notes that Ada Peter’s original and corrected declarations do not provide a specific date regarding when the summons and complaint were served on Defendant.  According to the proof of service filed on December 22, 2025, service was effectuated on October 22, 2025.  Now, Plaintiff claims that Ada Peter served the documents on a date “on or after” October 22, 2025.  The Court cannot ascertain when service was effectuated—whether it was served on October 22, 2025 as stated in the December 22, 2025 proof of service, sometime after October 22, 2025, or sometime in April 2026 after Mr. Shirwo presented his brown vehicle to Defendant’s business premises. 

 

Based on the ambiguities presented in the papers and at the hearing, the Court continued the hearing upon Plaintiff’s request for an evidentiary hearing.  The Court will make its determination on this motion at the evidentiary hearing.

 

However, if the parties have resolved this issue prior to the hearing, the parties should inform the Court and take the motion off-calendar.  If neither party appears to the evidentiary hearing, the Court would be inclined to grant the motion to quash service of the summons and complaint based on the record before it.  It appears that the parties do not contest that Mr. Mirimanyan is the agent for service of process for Defendant, Mr. Mirimanyan’s identity and physical features (as Defendant does not dispute that Mr. Mirimanyan was on the business premises on April 7 or 8 or that he is the person depicted in the photographs), or the business address, such that Plaintiff may re-attempt service on Defendant.
