ALLEGATIONS: 

 

A.     Operative Complaint

 

Yan Zhao and Tzen LLC (“Plaintiffs”), as member and manager, derivatively on behalf of New Regeneration Management LLC (“Company”), commenced this action against Defendants Oriternal Medical, LLC (“Oriternal”), Xiangdong Zhang (“Tony”), Xinze Zhang (“Arthur”), and Wei Wu, and named Company as a nominal defendant.  They bring this action individually for harms suffered as a member and manager of the Company or, alternatively, as a derivative shareholder suit arising from Plaintiffs’ rights under the Operating Agreement.  (FAC, ¶¶12-13.) 

 

On January 25, 2023, Zhao, Tony, and Boxian Wu formed a regenerative medicine clinic company initially named ADDZ Management LLC, which would be in charge of managing the day-to-day affairs of a regenerative medical clinic (the “clinic”).  (FAC, ¶¶18, 20.)  They agreed that Zhao would provide her expertise in managing regenerative medicine clinics and invest $25,000; Boxiang Wu would invest $200,000; and Tony would contribute the remainder.  (Id., ¶18.)  When drafting the Operating Agreement, Tony did not want to be listed as a member but placed his membership units under a company (Oriternal) owned by his son, Arthur.  (Id., ¶21.)  The Operating Agreement was entered in May 2023 by Plaintiffs, Oriternal, and Boxiang Wu wherein: (1) Tzen would own 10%, Boxiang Wu would own 20%, and Oriternal would own 70% of the membership units; (2) the Company would be manager-managed with Zhao as the manager for the general business affairs with no other member having authority or right to act on the Company’s  behalf; (3) matters under section 3.02 would require written approval of all members, including: entering into any series of transactions involving the sale of the Company or performing any acts that would make it impossible for the Company to carry out its ordinary business; (4) Oriternal would enter into the lease of the physical store on the Company’s behalf; (5) each member was permitted to access the Company’s corporate, financial, and similar records, reports, and documents; (6) Plaintiffs and any other sales representatives for the Company were entitled to receive monthly commissions; and (7) the Company’s profit and losses for each fiscal year would be allocated among the Members pro rata in accordance with their membership unit ownership percentage.  (Id., ¶¶22-23.) 

 

For nearly two years, Zhao dedicated time and energy into building the business without compensation.  (FAC, ¶24.)  As the clinic neared opening, individual Defendants began making business decisions that made it impossible for the Company to carry out its ordinary business, despite having no authority under the Operating Agreement.  (Id., ¶¶25-27.)

 

In March and July 2025, Defendants filed a statement of information for the Company listing Oriternal as the sole member and manager and an amendment to the Articles of Organization changing the name from ADDZ Management LLC to New Regeneration Management LLC, without member agreement or voting.  (Id., ¶27, Exs. C-D.)  Plaintiffs allege Defendants refused to recognize the Operating Agreement’s terms, appointed Wei Wu as the Company and clinic’s “business manager,” and hired several family members without member consent.  (Id., ¶27.) 

 

On December 17, 2025, the Company successfully opened, earning over $100,000 in its first month.  (FAC, ¶28.)  However, Plaintiffs allege that Tony unilaterally decided to sell the Company and took steps to prevent the Company and clinic from continuing operations, such as: (a) canceling training sessions for employees and temporarily laying off employees without the consent of all the Company’s members; (b) sending out appointment cancellation notices to patients scheduled at the clinic; (c) changing passwords for critical accounts needed to operate the business; (d) refusing to allow the clinic to set up a POS system; (e) refusing to return administrative access of the clinic’s EMR system back to the clinic as requested; (f) accessing and publicly releasing confidential patient records; and (g) refusing to pay the Company’s debts, salaries owed to employees, vendors payments, and monthly equipment payments.  (Id., ¶29.)  

 

The First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), filed June 24, 2026, alleges: (1) Breach of Fiduciary Duty; (2) Breach of Contract; (3) Tortious Interference with Contract; (4) Tortious Interference with Economic Relations; (5) Negligent Interference with Economic Relations; (6) Fraud; (7) Accounting; and (8) Declaratory Relief.

 

B.     Cross-Complaint

 

On June 3, 2026, Oriternal, Zhang, and Wu filed a Cross-Complaint (“Oriternal XC”) against Zhao, Tzen, H Badday Regenerative Medicine, Inc. (“HBRM”), and Hasan Badday, M.D. (“Dr. Badday”) for: (1) Declaratory Relief all Cross-Defendants; (2) Breach of Operating Agreement against Plaintiffs; (3) Breach of Management Services Agreement against HBRM; (4) Breach of Fiduciary Duty against Plaintiffs; (5) Aiding and Abetting Breach of Fiduciary Duty against Badday Cross-Defendants; (6)  Intentional Interference with Contractual Relations and/or Prospective Economic Relations (Pled in the Alternative) against HBRM Cross-Defendants; (7) Conversion against Plaintiffs and HBRM; (8) Unjust Enrichment/Restitution against all Cross-Defendants; (9) Accounting against all Cross-Defendants; (10) Judicial Dissociation/Expulsion of Member against Tzen; and (11) Constructive Trust against Plaintiffs. 

 

The Cross-Complaint alleges that New Regeneration Management LLC, f/k/a ADDZ Management LLC (the “Management Company”) was created to provide management service with a regenerative medical clinic, which operated in connection with the Management Company and HBRM.  (XC, ¶¶15-16.)  The Management Company is governed by the April 26, 2023 Operative Agreement (“OA”).  (Id., ¶17.)  Cross-Complainants allege Zhao and Tzen relied on the OA and Zha’s alleged manager/CEO status to claim authority over the Management Company.  (Id., ¶18.)  The Management Company and HBRM are parties to a written Management Services Agreement (“MSA”) dated February 16, 2023, wherein HBRM is the physician/practice side and ADDZ is the manager. (Id., ¶¶19-20, 22-23.)  Cross-Complainants assert they are not seeking control of the medical portions, but that their claims concern non-medical business operations only.  (Id., ¶21.)  Cross-Complainants are informed and believe that Zhao, Tzen, HBRM, and Dr. Badday used the physician-side authority and HBRM’s identity to bypass the agreed OA/MSA management structure and to redirect or control the non-medical business systems.  (Id., ¶¶24-31.) 

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On July 29, 2026, HBRM and Dr. Badday (together, “Badday Cross-Defendants”) filed a Demurrer to Oriternal’s Cross-Complaint.  On August 28, 2026, Cross-Complainants Oriternal, Tony, and Wei Wu filed an opposition.  On September 3, 2026, Badday Cross-Defendants filed a reply.

 

LEGAL STANDARD

 

The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters. (C.C.P. § 430.30(a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal. 3d 311, 318.) A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) The only issue involved in a demurrer hearing is whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Id.)

 

A demurrer assumes the truth of all factual, material allegations properly pled in the challenged pleading. (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at p. 318.) No matter how unlikely or improbable, the plaintiff’s allegations must be accepted as true for the purpose of ruling on the demurrer. (Del E. Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.  App. 3d 593, 604.) But this does not include contentions; deductions; conclusions of fact or law alleged in the complaint; facts impossible in law; or allegations contrary to facts of which a court may take judicial notice.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at 318.)

 

Pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 430.10(e) and (f), the party against whom a complaint has been filed may demur to the pleading on the grounds that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, or that the pleading is uncertain, ambiguous and/or unintelligible. It is an abuse of discretion to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is a reasonable probability that the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal. 4th 1074, 1082.)

 

MEET AND CONFER:

 

C.C.P. §§ 430.41(a) and 435.5(a) require that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the demurrer and/or motion to strike. Upon review, the Court finds the meet and confer requirements were met. (See Sparks Decl., ¶¶2-7.)  

 

ANALYSIS:

 

Badday Cross-Defendants demur to the First, Third, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Causes of Action in Oriternal’s Cross-Complaint.

 

A.     First Cause of Action for Declaratory Relief – Sustained with Leave to Amend  

 

A cause of action for declaratory relief is a remedy created by C.C.P. § 1060 and it is pleaded if it: (1) sets forth facts showing the existence of an actual controversy relating to the legal rights and duties of the respective parties and (2) requests that the rights and duties be adjudged.  (City of Tiburon v. Northwestern Pac. R.R. Co. (1970) 4 Cal.App.3d 160, 170; see C.C.P. § 1060 [identifying the remedy of declaratory relief].)  If these requirements are met, the Court must declare the rights of the parties whether or not the facts alleged establish that the plaintiff is entitled to a favorable declaration.  (Id.)  Declaratory relief is a broad remedy, and the rule that a complaint is to be liberally construed is particularly applicable to one for declaratory relief.  (Id.) 

 

The First Cause of Action alleges that an actual controversy exists between Cross-Complainants and Cross-Defendants concerning their respective rights, duties, and obligations under the Operating Agreement (“OA”), the Management Services Agreement (“MSA”), and related operational arrangements, including issues relating to authority, governance, access to systems and records, and control of business operations and assets.  (Oriternal XC, ¶47.)  Cross-Complainants seek a declaration that: (1) Zhao and Tzen may not rely on alleged manager or member authority to make unilateral decisions or changes outside the OA, outside the ordinary course of business, or adverse to the interests of the Management Company and its members; (2) HBRM may not use physician-side status, or HBRM accounts, systems, payroll, merchant accounts, POS systems, or EHR/practice-management access to bypass the MSA or impair the Management Company’s non-medical business-management rights; and (3) Dr. Badday may not personally authorize, ratify, or assist conduct that bypasses the OA/MSA structure or deprives Cross-Complainants of non-medical business records, systems, access, payment visibility, or operational information, except to the extent lawfully required to protect physician medical judgment and patient care.  (Id., ¶¶48-50.)  Cross-Complainants seek declarations concerning: (a) who presently has authority to act for or bind the Management Company; (b) what actions require written approval of all members; (c) whether Zhao may unilaterally alter payroll, banking, merchant accounts, POS, CareCredit, EHR/practice-management administrative access, email/domain credentials, records, vendors, or revenue systems; (d) whether HBRM may process or assume payroll, payment, merchant, CareCredit, or other non-medical business functions in a manner inconsistent with the MSA; and (e) whether Cross-Complainants are entitled to access and preserve records, logs, credentials, bank/merchant records, CareCredit records, payroll records, EHR/POS administrative logs, email/domain administrative logs, and other business records.  (Id., ¶51.) 

 

Badday Cross-Defendants argue that the Oriternal Cross-Complaint seeks a declaration that would illegally restrict and interfere with Dr. Badday’s medical practice and oversight of the Clinic owned and operated by HBRM.  They also argue that Cross-Complainants seek an advisory opinion relating to an alleged breach of the MSA by HBRM, where a matured action for money judgment would fully resolve the disputes. 

 

The Court declines to sustain the demurrer on this basis.  At this time, no declaration has been made by the Court that may affect Dr. Badday’s medical practice and oversight of the Clinic.  A demurrer is a procedurally inappropriate method for disposing of a complaint for declaratory relief.  (Lockheed Martin Corp. v. Continental Ins. Co. (2005) 134 Cal. App. 4th 187, 221.)  This is based on the reasoning that an order sustaining the demurrer would leave the parties where they were, with no binding determination of their rights, to await an actual breach and ensuing litigation.  (Id.)  This would defeat a fundamental purpose of declaratory relief, which is to remove uncertainties as to legal rights and duties before breach and without the risks and delays that it involves.  (Id.)  The object of declaratory relief is not necessarily a beneficial judgment; instead, it is a determination, favorable or unfavorable, that enables the plaintiff to act with safety.  (Id.)  This reasoning has established the rule that the defendant cannot, on demurrer, attack the merits of the plaintiff's claim (italics added for emphasis). (Id.)  Accordingly, a complaint is sufficient if it shows an actual controversy; it need not show that plaintiff is in the right.  (Id.) 

 

Next, Badday Cross-Defendants argue that Cross-Complainants have not identified an actual controversy over their own legal rights and duties such that they lack standing.  They contend that Zhang and Wu are not even alleged members of the Management Company, such that they have no conceivable basis to assert claims.  In opposition, Cross-Complainants argue that they can allege additional facts regarding standing or, alternatively, no additional facts are necessary because the Cross-Complaint already alleges that the MSA was signed for HBRM by Dr. Badday as medical director and signed for by ADDZ by Zhao, Tony, and Bo Xiong Wu as partners.  (Oriternal XC, ¶19.)  In the opposition, Cross-Complainants argue that the can allege additional facts regarding derivative claims and to restate entity-injury claims. 

 

Thus, the Court sustains the demurrer to the First Cause of Action with leave to amend so that Cross-Complainants may allege additional facts regarding standing. 

 

B.     Third Cause of Action for Breach of Management Services Agreement – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

The elements for breach of contract are: “(1) the existence of the contract, (2) plaintiff's performance or excuse for nonperformance, (3) defendant's breach, and (4) the resulting damages to plaintiff.”  (Oasis West Realty, LLC v. Goldman (2011) 51 Cal.4th 811, 821.) 

 

In the Third Cause of Action, Cross-Complainants allege that the MSA is a valid, enforceable, written agreement between HBRM and ADDZ (now New Regeneration) with respect to the management structure.  (Oriternal XC, ¶58.)  They are informed and believe that the Management Company has performed all conditions, covenants, and promises required under the MSA, or such performance has been excused by Cross-Defendants’ conduct.  (Id., ¶59.)  They allege the MSA requires HBRM to cooperate with the Management Company’s non-medical business-management functions, including functions related to staffing, payroll, accounting, billing, collections, payables, business records, systems, EHR access, payment handling, revenue flow, and operational administration, as well as requires HBRM not to obstruct, disrupt, interfere with, or impair the manager’s performance of its duties.  (Id., ¶50.)  They contend HBRM breached the MSA by: (a) allowing or enabling Zhao to bypass the Management Company’s non-medical business-management rights; (b) processing or attempting to process payroll, payments, merchant transactions, POS transactions, CareCredit transactions, or other business functions outside the agreed management structure; (c) restricting or impairing access to records, EHR/practice-management administrative information, logs, payment records, payroll records, and operational data; (d) using or allowing use of HBRM as a vehicle to reroute revenue, payroll, payment processing, or operational functions; (e) failing to provide or preserve access to books, records, systems, logs, and accounts required for the Management Company to perform its duties; and (f) obstructing, disrupting, interfering with, or impairing the Management Company’s performance under the MSA.  (Id., ¶61.)  They assert they were damaged, including loss of operational control, lost or diverted revenue, loss of visibility, forensic/accounting costs, restoration costs, and other consequential damages.  (Id., ¶62.) 

 

Badday Cross-Defendants argue that the Cross-Complaint identifies the parties to the MSA as HBRM and New Regeneration Management, LLC only.  They argue that the Cross-Complaint was not filed by New Regeneration Management, LLC, but instead was filed by Oriternal, Tony, and Wu, and that neither Zhang nor Wu are members of Oriternal.  Thus, Badday Cross-Defendants argue that Cross-Complainants lack standing to assert claims against HBRM.

 

In opposition, Cross-Complainants argue that they have alleged that Tony signed the MSA, such that the demurrer should be overruled as to him.  However, Cross-Complainants appear to acknowledge that they can amend the Cross-Complaint to cure any capacity defects.  Furthermore, the allegations do not allege any facts showing that HBRM breached any MSA terms as against Tony. 

 

In light of Cross-Complainants’ offer to amend the Cross-Complaint, the demurrer to the Third Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend.

 

C.     Fifth Cause of Action for Aiding and Abetting Breach of Fiduciary Duty – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

The Court of Appeal in American Master Lease LLC v. Idanta Partners, Ltd. (2014) 225 Cal.App.4th 1451 outlined two different theories pursuant to which a person may be liable for aiding and abetting a breach of fiduciary duty:

 

One theory, like conspiracy to breach a fiduciary duty, requires that the aider and abettor owe a fiduciary duty to the victim and requires only that the aider and abettor provide substantial assistance to the person breaching his or her fiduciary duty. [Citations.] On this theory, California law treats aiding and abetting a breach of fiduciary duty and conspiracy to breach a fiduciary duty similarly. Courts impose liability for concerted action that violates the aider and abettor's fiduciary duty. [Citations.] The second theory for imposing liability for aiding and abetting a breach of fiduciary duty arises when the aider and abettor commits an independent tort. [Citations.] This occurs when the aider and abettor makes “ ‘a conscious decision to participate in tortious activity for the purpose of assisting another in performing a wrongful act.’ ” [Citations.]

 

(American Master Lease LLC v. Idanta Partners, Ltd. (2014) 225 Cal.App.4th 1451, 1477 [citations omitted].)

 

In the Fifth Cause of Action, Cross-Complainants allege that Zhao owed fiduciary duties (as alleged in the Fourth Cause of Action).  (Oriternal XC, ¶70.)  Cross-Complainants are informed and believe that Badday Cross-Defendants had actual knowledge of Zhao’s claimed manager/CEO role, the existence of an internal management dispute, and the OA/MSA structure governing non-medical business operations.  (Id., ¶71.)  They are informed and believe that Badday Cross-Defendants provided substantial assistance or encouragement to Zhao’s breaches by authorizing or enabling Zhao to access, administer, use, or control bank accounts, payment-processing systems, POS systems, CareCredit/payment rails, EHR/practice management systems, payroll, revenue channels, or clinic operational systems outside the agreed management structure.  (Id., ¶72.)  Cross-Complainants believe that such assistance enabled Zhao and Tzen to bypass the Management Company’s non-medical management rights, restrict access to records and systems, and impair the interests of the Management Company and its members.  (Id., ¶73.) 

 

A review of the Fifth Cause of Action shows that, under the first theory, Cross-Complainants did not allege whether Badday Cross-Defendants owed Cross-Complainants a fiduciary duty to Cross-Complainants.  Next, under the second theory, Cross-Complainants did not allege facts that Badday Cross-Defendants engaged in an independent tort for the purpose of assisting Zhao in performing a wrongful act.  In opposition, Cross-Complainants represent that they can allege additional facts, relying on Zhao’s FAC allegations that Zhao obtained the Clinic doctor’s (or Dr. Badday) authorization to establish the Clinic’s bank account herself.  (See Opp. at pp.7-8.)

 

The demurrer to the Fifth Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend.

 

D.    Sixth Cause of Action for Intentional Interference with Contractual Relations and/or Prospective Economic Relations (Pled in the Alternative) – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

“The elements which a plaintiff must plead to state the cause of action for intentional interference with contractual relations are (1) a valid contract between plaintiff and a third party; (2) defendant's knowledge of this contract; (3) defendant's intentional acts designed to induce a breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; (4) actual breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; and (5) resulting damage.”  (Pac Gas & Electric Co. v. Bear Stearns & Co. (1990) 50 Cal.3d 1118, 1126.) 

 

The elements of the tort of intentional interference with prospective economic advantage are: “(1) an economic relationship between the plaintiff and some third party, with the probability of future economic benefit to the plaintiff; (2) the defendant's knowledge of the relationship; (3) intentional acts on the part of the defendant designed to disrupt the relationship; (4) actual disruption of the relationship; and (5) economic harm to the plaintiff proximately caused by the acts of the defendant.”  (Korea Supply Co. v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2003) 29 Cal.4th 1134, 1153.)  “In addition, the plaintiff must allege that the defendant's conduct was wrongful by some measure beyond the fact of the interference itself. [Citation.] In this context, an act is independently wrongful if it is unlawful, that is, if it is proscribed by some constitutional, statutory, regulatory, common law, or other determinable legal standard. [Citation.] The conduct must be independently actionable. The act of interference with prospective economic advantage is not tortious in and of itself, but requires pleading that a defendant has engaged in an act that was independently wrongful in order to distinguish lawful competitive behavior from tortious interference.”  (Stevenson Real Estate Services, Inc. v. CB Richard Ellis Real Estate Services, Inc. (2006) 138 Cal.App.4th 1215, 1220 [internal quotation marks and citations omitted].) 

 

The Sixth Cause of Action alleges that the OA and MSA are valid and enforceable contracts.  (Oriternal XC, ¶76.)  Cross-Complainants are informed and believe that Badday Cross-Defendants knew of the OA, MSA, and management structure created by those agreements, and that they intentionally engaged in conduct designed to disrupt or impair performance under the OA/MSA, including by enabling Zhao to bypass approval requirements, management rights, access rights, revenue controls, payroll processes, EHR/practice-management access, payment systems, and records obligations.  (Id., ¶¶77-78.)  Cross-Complainants are informed and believe that such conduct caused actual disruption or impairment of the OA and/or MSA, causing them to suffer damages.  (Id., ¶¶79-80.)  Alternatively, Cross-Complainants assert that to the extent HBRM is determined to be a contracting party to the MSA and therefore not capable of interfering with its own contract, this cause of action is directed at interference with the OA and/or at Dr. Badday to the extent he acted outside any protected agency capacity.  (Id., ¶81.) 

 

Badday Cross-Defendants argue that because HBRM is a party to the MSA, this claim cannot be alleged against a contracting party.  For this reason, the demurrer to the Intentional Inference with Contractual Relations Cause of Action is sustained as brought against HBRM. 

 

Next, Badday Cross-Defendants argue that Cross-Complainants are not parties to MSA, which was entered between HBRM and the Management Company only.  (Oriternal XC, ¶19.)  In opposition, Cross-Complainants argue that Oriternal has direct—not derivative—standing to assert this claim.   However, Cross-Complainants have not alleged a valid contract or an economic relationship between themselves and a third party to satisfy the elements of this claim as currently alleged.

 

With respect to the OA, the Cross-Complaint only alleges that the Management Company is governed by the OA, but makes no further allegations regarding the parties to the OA.  (See XC, ¶17.)  Thus, to the extent this cause of action relies on the OA’s terms, the allegations are uncertain. 

 

The demurrer to the Sixth Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend.  Additionally, for clarity purposes, Plaintiff should allege the Intentional Interference with Contractual Relations claim separately from the Intentional Interference with Prospective Economic Relations. 

 

E.     Seventh Cause of Action for Conversion – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

The elements for conversion are: (1) the plaintiff’s ownership or right to possession of the property; (2) the defendant’s conversion by a wrongful act or disposition of property rights, interfering with plaintiff’s possession; and (3) damages. (Lee v. Hanley (2015) 61 Cal.4th 1225, 1240; PCO, Inc. v. Christensen, Miller, Fink, Jacobs, Glaser, Weil & Shapiro, LLP (2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 384, 395.)  In this cause of action, it is necessary to show an assumption of control or ownership over the property, or that the alleged converter has applied the property to his own use.  (Shopoff & Cavallo LLP v. Hyon (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 1489, 1507.)

 

In the Seventh Cause of Action, Cross-Complainants allege they owned and/or had the immediate right to possess specific property and assets, including medical equipment, computers, patient records, business records, administrative credentials, system access, electronic business data, digital accounts, payment routing access, EHR/POS administrative logs, payroll records, merchant records, and other company property.  (XC, ¶83.)  They assert Cross-Defendants wrongfully exercised dominion and control over such property and assets by seizing, withholding, rerouting, controlling, concealing, transferring, impairing, or denying access to the same, without Cross-Complainants’ consent.  (Id., ¶84.)  They are informed and believe that Cross-Defendants wrongfully controlled and exercised dominion over identifiable funds held in merchant accounts and/or other identifiable accounts associated with Cross-Complainants’ business operations.  (Id., ¶85.)  Cross-Complainants allegedly owned, possessed, and/or had the immediate right to possess the Removed Property, which constituted specific, identifiable personal property located at the Clinic immediately prior to Zhao’s removal of it on May 16, 2026, including medical equipment, computers, patient records, skincare products, vitamins, refrigerated medications, and other business property.  (Id., ¶86.)  Cross-Complainants contend that by removing the Removed Property from the Clinic without notice to Cross-Complainants or the other owners, and by failing to provide an inventory or disclose the Removed Property’s location, Zhao exercised dominion and control over the Removed Property in a manner inconsistent with Cross-Complainants’ rights.  (Id., ¶87.) 

 

Badday Cross-Defendants argue that Cross-Complainants have not alleged facts regarding their ownership or right to possess the subject property, or facts that HBRM exercised dominion or control. 

 

In opposition, Cross-Complainants request leave to amend to assert HBRM’s dominion and to restate the claim derivatively as company-owned property.  (Opp. at p.9.)

 

As such, the demurrer to the Seventh Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend.

 

F.     Eighth Cause of Action for Unjust Enrichment/Restitution – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

Under California law, unjust enrichment is not a cause of action.  (Melchior v. New Line Productions, Inc. (2003) 106 Cal. App. 4th 779, 794.)  Instead, it is the failure to make restitution under circumstances where it is equitable to do so.  (Id.)  Unjust enrichment is a general principle, underlying various legal doctrines and remedies, rather than a remedy itself.  (Id.)  It is synonymous with restitution.  (Id.)  This is the basis for the general rule in California, which finds that unjust enrichment is not a cause of action, but a claim for restitution.  (Hill v. Roll Int'l Corp. (2011) 195 Cal. App. 4th 1295, 1307.)

 

In opposition, Cross-Complainants request that the Court allow them to restate this claim as a common count claim for money had and received. 

 

The demurrer to the Eighth Cause of Action is sustained because there is no cause of action for unjust enrichment.  However, the Court will allow leave to amend so that Cross-Complainants may restate this claim as a claim for common counts.

 

G.    Ninth Cause of Action for Accounting – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

“A cause of action for an accounting requires a showing that a relationship exists between the plaintiff and defendant that requires an accounting, and that some balance is due the plaintiff that can only be ascertained by an accounting.”  (Teselle v. McLoughlin (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 156, 179.)  “An action for accounting is not available where the plaintiff alleges the right to recover a sum certain or a sum that can be made certain by calculation.”  (Id.)

 

In the Ninth Cause of Action, Cross-Complainants allege that the financial transactions at issue are complex and involve records not fully available to Cross-Complainants, including bank accounts, merchant accounts, POS systems, CareCredit/payment rails, cash collections, payroll records, EHR/practice-management records, vendor records, and HBRM-related financial records.  (XC, ¶94.)  Cross-Complainants contend they invested over $2,000,000 into the development, buildout, equipment acquisition, lease obligations, staffing, and operational infrastructure of the clinic business, the accounting and disposition of which is not fully known and requires review of complete financial records.  (Id.)  They are informed and believe that Cross-Defendants possess or control information necessary to determine revenues received, funds diverted, expenses incurred, payroll processed, assets transferred, and benefits retained.  (Id., ¶95.) They seek an accounting of all funds, revenues, patient payments, merchant/POS proceeds, CareCredit proceeds, cash, payroll transactions, vendor payments, receivables, and other financial transactions associated with the clinic and Management Company during the relevant period.  (Id., ¶96.) 

 

Badday Cross-Defendants argue that the Cross-Complaint lacks facts that they had any relationship with Cross-Complainants, as HBRM and the Management Company are the only parties to the MSA.  In opposition, Cross-Complainants argue that they can state this claim derivatively.   As such, the Court sustains the demurrer to the Ninth Cause of Action with leave to amend. 

 

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Cross-Defendants H Badday Regenerative Medicine, Inc. and Hasan Badday, M.D.’s Demurrer came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows:  

 

The Demurrer to the CROSS-complaint iS SUSTAINED WITH 30 DAYS’ LEAVE TO AMEND AS TO THE FIRST, THIRD, FIFTH, SIXTH, Seventh, Eighth, AND NINTH CAUSES OF ACTION. 

 

CROSS-Defendant HBRM TO GIVE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.


Case Number: 26NNCV01980    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 26NNCV01980

 

MP:     Defendant Brandt Stites

RP:      Plaintiffs Bay Cities Law Group, Inc. and Steven Zelig

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Bay Cities Law Group, Inc. (“BCLG”) and Steven Zelig (“Mr. Zelig”) (together, “Plaintiffs”) allege that in 2019, the home of Lynn B. Stites (“Decedent”) and Defendant Erma Lee Miller, individually (“Miller”) and as Decedent’s successor in interest, was vandalized by their biological daughter, Sonia, such that they made an insurance claim to State Farm on behalf of Miller, Decedent, and their granddaughter “TR.”  (Compl., ¶8.)  Plaintiffs allege that in 2019 until the Underlying Action was filed in mid-2020, legal aspects of the insurance claim were pursued by Decedent and aided and abetted by Glenn Murphy (Miller’s son, “Mr. Murphy”) and Litigation Advocacy Group (“LAG”) (together, “Murphy Defendants”).  (Id., ¶9.)  Plaintiffs allege Decedent and Murphy Defendants mishandled the Miller et al. v. State Farm case (LASC Case No. 20BBCV00479; hereinafter, “Underlying Action”), thereby negatively impacting the claim and lawsuit against State Farm.  (Id., ¶10.)  In August 2020, Murphy Defendants filed the Underlying Action on behalf of Miller, Decedent, and TR, but Plaintiffs now are informed and believe that Decedent ghost-wrote the pleadings, litigation-related documents, and letters to State Farm to create the appearance that they were written by Miller; Decedent practiced law without a license and after disbarment; Decedent was aided and abetted by Miller and Murphy Defendants; and Miller aided and abetted Decedent’s unauthorized and illegal practice of law.  (Id., ¶¶11-12.) 

 

In early/mid-2023, Mr. Murphy recruited Plaintiffs to take over representation of the Millers.  (Compl., ¶14.)  In fall 2023, Decedent passed away and his claims were taken over by Miller as successor with Murphy Defendants as attorneys of record in the Underlying Action.  (Id., ¶15.)  Plaintiffs allege Murphy Defendants failed to adequately represent the Millers, failed to obtain and preserve key evidence, and abandoned representing Miller and TR after Decedent’s death.  (Id., ¶16.)  In August 2024, Miller (individually and as Decedent’s successor in interest) entered into a fee agreement for handling the Underlying Action with BCLG.  (Id., ¶¶17-18.)  BCLG, through Mr. Zelig and other employees, invested time in the Underlying Action.  (Id., ¶19.) 

 

During BCLG’s representation, Defendant Brandt Stites (Miller’s other son, “Mr. Stites”) falsely held himself out to Mr. Zelig as a licensed attorney and volunteered his time, never requested a fee, and was not a part of any fee or fee-splitting agreement.  (Compl., ¶20.)  Plaintiffs later learned that Mr. Stites received his law license in late January 2025 outside of California.  (Id.) 

 

In mid-2025, as a result of Plaintiffs’ representation, the Underlying Action settled for a confidential amount.  (Compl., ¶22.)  Plaintiffs allege that Defendants fabricated a dispute and records to cheat BCLG of their fees, asserted that the fee agreement was unconscionable, made false accusations against Mr. Zelig that he conducted himself abusively with TR, and asserted that BCLG waived its right to fees.  (Id., ¶¶22-24, 27, 30.) 

 

By way of this action, Plaintiffs seek to compel arbitration against Miller pursuant to the attorney-client fee agreement, and for declaratory relief and damages against the Murphy Defendants and Mr. Stites in this civil action.  (Compl., ¶¶1-2.)

 

The Complaint, filed March 18, 2026, alleges: (1) an Order Compelling Arbitration by Plaintiffs against Miller, individually and as Decedent’s successor in interest; (2) Declaratory Relief by Plaintiffs against Mr. Murphy, LAG, and Mr. Stites; (3) Conversion by BCLG against Mr. Murphy, LAG, and Mr. Stites; and (4) Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress by Zelig against Mr. Murphy, LAG, and Mr. Stites. 

 

On August 21, 2026, Plaintiffs dismissed without prejudice the Third and Fourth Causes of Action against Murphy Defendants (Mr. Murphy and LAG) only. 

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On July 20, 2026, Brandt Stites (“in pro per, with assistance from Litigation Advocacy Group”) filed a Special Anti-SLAPP Motion to Strike Plaintiffs’ Complaint.  On August 31, 2026, Plaintiffs filed an untimely opposition which the Court will consider.  On September 3, 2026, Mr. Stites filed a reply.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

C.C.P. § 425.16 provides a two-step test in determining whether a cause of action constitutes a SLAPP. (Navellier v. Sletten (2002) 29 Cal.4th 82, 88; C.C.P. § 425.16(b)(1).) “Only a cause of action that satisfies both prongs … is a SLAPP, subject to being stricken under the statute.” (Navellier, supra, 29 Cal.4th at 89.)

 

First, the defendant must make the threshold showing that the challenged cause of action arises from protected speech or petition activity. (City of Cotati v. Cashman (2002) 29 Cal.4th 69, 76.) “[T]he statutory phrase ‘cause of action...arising’ from means simply that the defendant's act underlying the plaintiff's cause of action must itself have been an act in furtherance of the right of petition or free speech.” (Id. at 78.) This step is satisfied if the defendant shows that the challenged claims arise from one of the four protected activities provided under C.C.P. § 425.16(e).  (Id.) 

 

Second, [i]f the court finds such a showing has been made, it then must determine whether the plaintiff has demonstrated a probability of prevailing on the claim.”  (Navellier, supra, 29 Cal.4th at 88.)  To meet this second step, the plaintiff must demonstrate: (1) “that the complaint is both legally sufficient” and (2) “supported by a sufficient prima facie showing of facts to sustain a favorable judgment if the evidence submitted by the plaintiff is credited.” (Id. at 89 [internal quotation marks omitted].)

 

In analyzing the second step, the court considers “the pleadings, and supporting and opposing affidavits stating the facts upon which the liability or defense is based.” (C.C.P. § 425.16(b)(2).)  The evidentiary showing by the plaintiff must be made by competent and admissible evidence.  (Morrow v. Los Angeles Unified Sch. Dist. (2007) 149 Cal.App.4th 1424, 1444; Evans v. Unkow (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 1490, 1497-98 [proof cannot be made by declaration based on information and belief]; Tuchscher Dev. Enters., Inc. v. San Diego Unified Port Dist. (2003) 106 Cal.App.4th 1219, 1236-38 [documents submitted without proper foundation could not be considered in determining plaintiff's probability of prevailing on its claim].)  However, “[l]ooking at those affidavits, [the courts] do not weigh credibility, nor...evaluate the weight of the evidence. Instead [the courts] accept as true all evidence favorable to the plaintiff and assess the defendant's evidence only to determine if it defeats the plaintiff's submission as a matter of law.” (Grewal v. Jammu (2011) 19 Cal.App.4th 977, 989 [internal quotation marks omitted].) 

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     Plaintiffs’ Objection to the Motion

 

“The special motion may be filed within 60 days of the service of the complaint or, in the court's discretion, at any later time upon terms it deems proper. The motion shall be scheduled by the clerk of the court for a hearing not more than 30 days after the service of the motion unless the docket conditions of the court require a later hearing.”  (C.C.P. § 425.16(f).)  “Section 425.16, subdivision (f), however, does not require a moving defendant to request leave of court prior to filing an untimely motion. Instead, subdivision (f) authorizes the court, in its discretion, to consider an untimely motion without restriction as to whether or when the moving defendant so requests.”  (Chitsazzadeh v. Kramer & Kaslow (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 676, 684.) 

 

The Proof of Service of Summons, filed April 16, 2026, shows that the summons and complaint were personally served on Brandt Stites on April 11, 2026 at 1:43 p.m. at 1229 Dedi Ave., South Lake Tahoe, CA 96150.  Sixty days from the April 11, 2026 service date is June 10, 2026.

 

In their untimely opposition, Plaintiffs object to the entirety of the motion, arguing that it was not timely filed because Mr. Stites’ motion was filed almost 100 days after service and he did not obtain the Court’s permission for the late filing. 

 

Mr. Stites was personally served on April 11, 2026, such that he was required to file a special motion to strike by June 10, 2026 (60 days).  However, the motion was filed on July 20, 2026, which is the 100th day.  As such, it is untimely unless the Court exercises its discretion to allow the late filing.

 

The following background is relevant. 

 

On May 8, 2026, Mr. Stites filed a Declaration of Demurring or Moving Party in Support of Automatic Extension.  He states that on May 4, 2026, he drafted an email to Mr. Zelig to meet and confer but discovered his email was in the draft folder; and he thereafter edited the email and sent it to Mr. Zelig.  Mr. Stites declares that on May 8, 2026, Mr. Zelig responded, standing by the pleadings and requesting a response.  Mr. Stites then states: “Thereafter, upon further review, Mr. Zelig's Complaint appears to be the proper subject of a special anti-SLAPP motion to strike. Accordingly, I respectfully request a statutory 60-day extension of time to prepare an anti-SLAPP motion for filing by July 10, 2026. Additionally, the requested extension is warranted to provide sufficient time to seek local counsel, as Mr. Zelig served me at my residence in Lake Tahoe and local counsel in Los Angeles is needed to assist me.” 

 

On July 16, 2026, the Court entered Murphy Defendants and Plaintiffs’ Stipulation and Order Extending Time to File a Responsive Pleading, ordering that Murphy Defendants may file a responsive pleading to the Complaint up to and including July 31, 2026.  The Court notes that there was no mention of Mr. Stites in the Stipulation and Order.

 

On August 18, 2026, the Court entered Murphy Defendants and Plaintiffs’ Amended Stipulation and Order Extending Time to File a Responsive Pleading, ordering that Plaintiffs provide Miller’s client file in the matter Miller et al. v. State Farm (LASC Case No. 20BBCV00479) to counsel for Murphy Defendants by July 26, 2026; Murphy Defendants may file a responsive pleading to the Complaint, including a Special Motion to Strike, by September 11, 2026; and the other was not to be construed as a waiver of Murphy Defendants’ rights to respond by demurrer, motion to strike, special motion to strike, answer, or any other authorized pleading.  Again, the Court notes that there was no mention of Mr. Stites in the Amended Stipulation and Order. 

 

While Mr. Stites’ Declaration of Demurring or Moving Party in Support of Automatic Extension includes a request to file his motion by July 10, 2026, it also shows that he did not make this request to Plaintiffs or seek a Court order.  Furthermore, even if such a request were granted by way of the Declaration, Mr. Stites filed his motion on July 20, 2026, which is ten days after his requested filing deadline of July 10, 2026.

 

Next, the Court notes that it entered two separate Stipulations and Orders Extending Time to File a Responsive Pleading.  The Stipulations/Orders defined “Defendants” to include only Glenn Murphy and Litigation Advocacy Group; mention of Mr. Stites was absent from these orders.  Furthermore, Mr. Stites is a self-represented litigant (as an out-of-state attorney) who appears to have the “assistance of” LAG, but he is not represented by LAG and there is no substitution of attorney form filed that LAG is representing Mr. Stites (before or at the time of the Stipulations/Orders). 

 

Nevertheless, as stated in Chitsazzadeh, section 425.16(f) does not require Mr. Stites to have requested leave of Court prior to filing the untimely motion.  While this may have been a matter of professional courtesy to the parties and the Court, the Court may exercise its discretion to consider the untimely filed motion regardless of whether he requested an extension. 

 

As Plaintiffs have substantively opposed Mr. Stites’ motion following their objection based on untimeliness, the Court will exercise its discretion and consider the substantive merits of the motion.  As such, Plaintiffs’ objection is overruled.

 

B.     Prong 1:  Arising from Protected Activity – Mr. Stites’ Initial Burden

 

Mr. Stites addresses each cause of action directed against him, arguing that they arise from protected petition activities.

 

1.      Second Cause of Action for Declaratory Relief

 

Although Mr. Stites does not cite a specific subsection of C.C.P. § 425.16(e) for the basis of his initial burden and he generally refers to the claims as arising from acts in furtherance of his rights to petition, the Court assumes that Mr. Stites is basing his motion on the Declaratory Relief Cause of Action on C.C.P. § 425.16(e)(1) and (2), which defines “act in furtherance of a person’s right of petition or free speech under the United States or California Constitution in connection with at public issues” as: “(1) any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other official proceeding authorized by law” or “(2) any written or oral statement or writing made in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or judicial body, or any other official proceeding authorized by law.”  (C.C.P. § 425.16(e)(1)-(2).)  (The Court does not find subsections (3) or (4) applicable as this action does not involve a public issue or an issue of public interest.)

 

The Second Cause of Action for Declaratory Relief by Plaintiffs against all Defendants alleges: “Defendants … have asserted false and baseless claims against the specific funds. BCLG contends that the claims are frivolous and without basis and are designed to literally … cheat Plaintiff out of funds to which it is entitled. Accordingly, an actual controversy exists between Plaintiff and the Defendants named in this cause of action.”  (Compl., ¶40.)  Plaintiffs request orders to the effect that Defendants have no valid claims against Plaintiffs and/or the funds held in trust.  (Id., ¶41.) 

 

Mr. Stites argues that Plaintiffs’ Second Cause of Action for Declaratory Relief arises from Mr. Stites’ protected petitioning activity because it seeks to stop the act of filing any claims against Plaintiffs and/or the funds held in their trust account.  (Mot. at p.7.)  He states in his declaration that when Mr. Zelig threatened to sue him, he told Miller that he was seriously contemplating his right to assert claims against Plaintiffs for all the litigation-related activities he performed for Plaintiffs in the Underlying State Farm case, but despite the Complaint’s false allegations, he never filed claims against Plaintiffs or the 38% fee Mr. Zelig took from Miller’s settlement.  (Mr. Stites Decl., ¶19.) 

 

With respect to the Second Cause of Action, the Court finds that Mr. Stites has not established his initial burden.  Plaintiffs’ Complaint does not allege facts regarding whether Mr. Stites made written or oral statements before a judicial proceeding or in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a judicial body.   At most, Plaintiffs alleged:

 

27. After the “confidential” settlement, the Millers, individually and acting by and through the Murphy Defendants and B. Stites, maliciously and without basis whatsoever fabricated the following with the goal of cheating BCLG:

 

a. That the Fee Agreement freely negotiated by the Murphy Defendants was unconscionable even though Murphy was a licensed attorney who specialized in a statutory claims, and who admitted perfecting the mechanics of charging unconscionable fees and even though, objectively, there was absolutely nothing unconscionable or inappropriate about the Fee Agreement. In fact, the fee percentages and other provisions in the Fee Agreement were “below market.”

 

b. Very revealingly, until after a very favorable settlement was achieved with State Farm, Defendants never took the position that any aspect of the Fee Agreement, negotiated and approved by Murphy and presumably B. Stites, was improper.

 

c. Other profoundly nasty, arbitrary, vile, despicable and malicious tactics and accusations according to proof.

 

(Compl., ¶27.)  Plaintiffs did not allege facts that Mr. Stites made any statements in connection with a court proceeding, that he threatened litigation, filed a lawsuit, etc.  Rather, Mr. Stites’ states in his own declaration that while he contemplated asserting his rights, he never filed claims against Plaintiffs or for fees.  (Mr. Stiles Decl., ¶19.)  Based on the allegations of the Complaint, it appears that after settling the Underlying Action, the parties had a private disagreement about the amount of fees Plaintiffs were entitled to under the BCLG Fee Agreement, but such disagreements were not made as a part of or before any judicial proceedings but occurred after the Underlying Action had settled.  (See Drell v. Cohen (2014) 232 Cal.App.4th 24, 30 [“None of the purposes of the anti-SLAPP statute would be served by elevating a fee dispute to the constitutional arena, thereby requiring a party seeking a declaration of rights under an attorney lien to demonstrate a probability of success on the merits in order to obtain equitable relief.”].) 

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs too cite to Mr. Stiles’ declaration at paragraph 19, stating: “if Stites is willing to state on the record that he is not making any claims against the fee, then Plaintiffs will happily dismiss this cause of action against him. However, absent that, Plaintiffs request a declaration from the court.”  (Opp. at 4:16-18.) 

 

In considering a special motion to strike, the issues are framed by the pleadings.  “If there are no acts alleged, there can be no showing that alleged acts arise from protected activity. And, if there cannot be such a showing, the first prong is not satisfied and the anti-SLAPP motion must be denied.”  (Central Valley Hospitalists v. Dignity Health (2018) 19 Cal.App.5th 203, 214; see also id. at 2818-219 [upholding trial court’s finding that if there are no acts alleged, there can be no showing that the alleged acts arise from protected activity, and that the trial court could not accept evidence based solely on what the defendant believed plaintiff’s claims are based on].)  As stated in Medical Marijuana, Inc. v. ProjectCBD.com (2016) 6 Cal.App.5th 602, 621:

 

It would be inappropriate for us to insert into a pleading claims for relief based on allegations of activities that plaintiffs simply have not identified, even if the parties suggest on appeal how plaintiffs might have intended to frame those claims or attempt to identify the specific conduct or assertions of statements alleged to be false on which plaintiffs intended to base such claims for relief.[] It is not our role to engage in what would amount to a redrafting of the first amended complaint in order to read that document as alleging conduct that supports a claim that has not in fact been specifically alleged, and then assess whether the pleading that we have essentially drafted could survive the anti-SLAPP motion directed at it. … Where, as here, the operative complaint alleges no act on the part of the moving defendants in support of the claim or claims for relief that those defendants seek to strike from that complaint, defendants are not entitled to strike those claims for relief pursuant to the anti-SLAPP statute, although they may have other remedies available to them to address deficiencies in the pleading.

 

(Medical Marijuana, Inc. v. ProjectCBD.com (2016) 6 Cal.App.5th 602, 621.)

 

Thus, the motion is denied as to the Second Cause of Action for Declaratory Relief because Mr. Stites did not meet his initial burden. 

 

2.      Third Cause of Action for Conversion

 

In the Third Cause of Action for Conversion by BCLG against Mr. Stites, BCLG alleges it had a right to possess specific identifiable funds owed to it (which it claims is confidential pursuant to the settlement entered between the Millers and State Farm). (Compl., ¶43.)  BCLG contends that Mr. Stites intentionally and knowingly interfered with BCLG’s right to possess the specific fund, and he knew his position was frivolous and undertaken with malice.  (Id., ¶44.)  BCLG did not consent to the prevention of access to the specific funds and Mr. Stites’ intentional conduct was a substantial factor in causing BCLG’s damages.  (Id., ¶45.)  BCLG asserts it suffered substantial economic losses, including, but not limited to: (a) loss of access to specific funds, per se; (b) loss of the ability to invest the funds; (c) loss of the ability to utilize the funds in constructive and positive ways; (d) loss of interest on the funds at the legal rate; and (e) other economic losses according to proof.  (Id., ¶46.) 

 

Again, Mr. Stites does not cite to any specific subsection under C.C.P. § 425.16(e).  At most, he argues that Plaintiffs’ Conversion claim, just like the Declaratory Relief claim, arises from trying to stop Mr. Stites’ act of asserting any valid claims against Mr. Zelig or the funds held in his trust account.  (Mot. at p.7.)  Mr. Stites argues he never entered into a fee agreement for the funds, was not a party to the State Farm case, and the only way he could interfere with Mr. Zelig’s right to the funds was if he asserted a legal claim for the 38% of funds held in Mr. Zelig’s trust account—which he claims is what Plaintiffs’ Declaratory Relief and Conversion Causes of Action seek to prevent.  (Id. at pp.7-8.) 

 

For the same reasons discussed with respect to the Declaratory Relief Cause of Action, the Court finds that Mr. Stites has not upheld his initial burden on the Conversion Cause of Action. 

 

Furthermore, as pointed out by Plaintiffs, the Conversion claim’s facts arose after the Underlying Action was resolved.  (Opp. at 5:19-21; see Compl., ¶¶43-46.)  Thus, Mr. Stites has not shown that, as framed by the pleadings, that he engaged in protected petitioning activity with respect to the funds.  In contrast, he states that he took no action on the funds at all.  (See Mr. Stites Decl., ¶19.)

 

As such, Mr. Stites did not meet his initial burden on the Third Cause of Action for Conversion.   The motion is accordingly denied as to the Third Cause of Action. 

 

3.      Fourth Cause of Action for IIED

 

In the Fourth Cause of Action for IIED by Mr. Zelig against Mr. Stites, Mr. Zelig alleges that Mr. Stites intended to inflict substantial emotional distress on Mr. Zelig or engaged in misconduct (including extortion) with reckless disregard for the probable consequences.  (Compl., ¶50.)  He alleges Mr. Stites knew there was no basis to accuse Mr. Zelig of abusing TR or to dispute any aspect of BCLG’s fee and cost reimbursement request, but Mr. Stites maliciously threatened to submit a false administrative claim against Mr. Zelig to the  State Bar of California unless Plaintiffs agreed to take nothing for attorney fees and/or unreimbursed costs, knowing that the false report to the State Bar was upsetting on its face and posed a threat to Mr. Zelig’s livelihood notwithstanding its patent invalidity.  (Id., ¶50.)  Mr. Zelig asserts that he suffered substantial economic loss as a proximate result of Mr. Stites’ conduct in engaging in extortion per se and/or aiding and abetting the same.  (Id., ¶51.) 

 

With respect to claims that Mr. Stites accused Mr. Zelig of conducting himself abusively towards TR, the Court notes that Mr. Stites did not address this allegation in the motion and whether it constituted protected petitioning activity, under any of the C.C.P. § 425.16(e) prongs (such as whether this was in connection with a judicial proceeding or if the abuse of a minor is a matter of public interest, etc.).  It is unclear where such statements were made and for what purpose.  (See Compl., ¶¶24, 50.) 

 

With respect to claims that Mr. Stites threatened to report Mr. Zelig to the California State Bar unless Plaintiffs agreed to take no attorney’s fees and costs (i.e., extortion), Mr. Stites argues that he has established his initial burden, relying on Barry v. State Bar of California (2017) 2 Cal.5th 318.  (Barry, supra, 2 Cal.5th at 322 [“At the first step of the analysis, the trial court concluded that all of Barry's claims concerned the State Bar's actions in pursuing charges against Barry and recommending to this court that she be disciplined, and thus arose from protected petitioning activity.”].)  He argues that any claims based on Mr. Stites’ alleged statements that he was “acting through” Miller was during pre-lawsuit settlement negotiations to settle the dispute about funds.  (Opp. at p.10.) 

 

In Cohen v. Brown (2009) 173 Cal.App.4th 302, defendants attorney Michael Brown and his law firm associated the plaintiff as counsel in an underlying personal injury lawsuit.  (Id. at 307.)  However, Brown did not disclose to the plaintiff that Brown’s license had been suspended, which prevented him from practicing law.  (Id.)  Brown informed the plaintiff that Brown would receive 40% of the verdict/settlement in the underlying action pursuant to a contingency fee agreement.  (Id.)  The plaintiff and defendants agreed to a fee sharing agreement, which Brown represented to the plaintiff had been disclosed to the client.  (Id. at 308.)  The plaintiff conducted a substantial amount of work but a week prior to mediation, Brown dismissed plaintiff’s services.  (Id. at 310.)  The plaintiff then filed an attorney’s lien.  (Id.)  Brown then retained another attorney to represent the client in settlement negotiations, and the case settled. (Id.)  The plaintiff’s complaint alleged that Brown wrote to plaintiff that he would file a complaint with the State Bar if the plaintiff did not sign off on the settlement check and permit the entire attorney’s fees to go to Brown and, thereafter, Brown filed a false complaint with the State Bar against the plaintiff over the client’s name, resulting in the initiation of an inquiry by the State Bar.  (Id. at 310-311.)  Brown filed a special motion to strike the plaintiff’s complaint, arguing the plaintiff retaliated against Brown for assisting the client to file a complaint with the State Bar and successfully representing the client in the underlying lawsuit and collecting his fees.  (Id. at 312.)  The trial court denied defendants attorney Michael Brown and the law firm’s special motion to strike the plaintiff’s complaint, finding that Brown’s activities were not acts taken by Brown as a valid exercise of his rights of petition or free speech, but rather constituted extortion and were therefore illegal.  (Id. at 306, 315.) 

 

The Court of Appeal affirmed.  “It is well settled that extortion is not constitutionally protected speech and thus cannot constitute the ‘valid’ exercise of speech and petition that is protected by section 425.16.”  (Cohen, supra, 173 Cal.App.4th at 317.)  Furthermore, California Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 5–100 states in relevant part: “A member shall not threaten to present criminal, administrative, or disciplinary charges to obtain an advantage in a civil dispute.”  (Id.)  The Court of Appeal found that not only did Brown threaten to present administrative charges, he actually presented administrative charges to the State Bar, through his client, and Brown’s communications with the plaintiff demonstrated that the purpose of filing the State Bar complaint was to gain an advantage in the underlying lawsuit by pressuring plaintiff into immediately signing off on the settlement check, and to make the plaintiff’s life a “living hell” until he did so.  (Id.)  Thus, while Brown asserted that his motion that the State Bar complaint was about Zerah receiving his share of settlement funds and not about Brown receiving attorney’s fees, the Court of Appeal found that such position was inconsistent with the evidence.  (Id. at 318.)  Thus, the Court found that the record showed Brown’s actions with respect to the filing of the State Bar complaint constituted extortion.  It cited Flatley v. Mauro (2006) 39 Cal.4th 299, noting that “(1) the threat made by an extortionist does not have to succeed in producing an exchange of money in order to constitute extortion; (2) the action that is threatened unless money is paid may itself not be an illegal action but instead, it is the coupling of the threat of that action with the demand for money that constitutes the illegality; and (3) it is immaterial to the crime of extortion that the purpose of the threat is to collect money justly due the extortionist.”  (Id. at 318.)  The Court of Appeal concluded that Brown’s “assistance” to the client in filing the State Bar complaint did not insulate him and determined that his stated basis for relief under section 425.16 was not viable, such that the court need not reach whether plaintiff made a prima facie showing on prevailing on the merits. (Id.) 

 

In the Complaint, Plaintiffs allege: “Miller, acting individually and expressly through her ‘two attorney sons,’ then took it up a further malicious and extortive notch. More specifically, Defendants then made it clear that unless Plaintiffs relinquished the right to any payment (and gave the Millers the entire gross settlement amount) that they would maliciously report Plaintiffs to the State Bar even though there was no basis for such a report. This constituted extortion per se and was designed specifically designed to upset and intimidate Zelig. In fact, Defendants were successful in causing Zelig substantial and enduring emotional distress.”  (Compl., ¶31.) 

 

However, Mr. Stites states that he never threatened to report Mr. Zelig to the California State Bar and that he did not know that Miller called the California State Bar to complain about Mr. Zelig until after she had already done so.  (Mr. Stites Decl., ¶18.)  He states that Miller and TR then decided on their own to lodge formal complaints against Mr. Zelig with the California State Bar.  (Id.) 

 

Miller provides her declaration, stating that after Mr. Zelig spoke with TR over the phone regarding the Minor’s Compromise Petition, she decided to call the California Bar about Mr. Zelig’s unethical conduct and that she and TR decided on their own, and without talking to her attorney sons, to file complaints about Mr. Zelig’s unethical conduct to the Stat Bar.  (Miller Decl., ¶29.)  She states that before State Farm sent the total settlement funds to Mr. Zelig’s trust account, she learned that Mr. Murphy that told Mr. Zelig that she had agreed to Mr. Zelig’s offer to take 25% of the settlement funds.  (Id., ¶33.)  Miller states that though she had already called the State Bar to complaint that Mr. Zelig’s 25% fee was unconscionable, she did not want to give Mr. Zelig a reason to follow through with his threats to sue her attorney sons unless she agreed to his demand.  (Id.)  Minor TR similarly states that after the Minor’s Compromise Petition process, she and Miller decided on their own to report Mr. Zelig to the California Bar and file complaints to the State Bar about the things he did when he was their attorney in the Underlying Action.  (TR Decl., ¶8.) 

 

In response, Mr. Zelig addresses Miller’s declaration statements in his own declaration.  To Miller’s paragraph 29, he argues that Miller did not specify the date she called the State Bar or filed written complaints, nor included a copy of the complaint.  (Zelig Decl., ¶19.)  Mr. Zelig states without any supporting facts: “I may be wrong, but I do not believe Miller is telling the truth.”  (Id.)  With respect to Miller’s paragraph 33, he states he made multiple attempts to resolve the fee dispute, but Defendants often did not respond.  (Id., ¶21.) 

 

Based on the allegations of the Fourth Cause of Action, the Court finds that Mr. Stites has established his initial burden in showing that his alleged activities of threatening to file a claim with the State Bar constituted protected activity.  The Court does not find that, based on Plaintiffs’ allegations, that the Flatley/Cohen exception regarding extortion has been established to take this claim out of the protection of the anti-SLAPP statute.  Plaintiffs’ allegations do not allege sufficient facts regarding extortion, other than to state in a conclusory manner that Mr. Stites’ conduct amounts to “extortion per se.”  Furthermore, the evidence submitted by the parties shows that Mr. Stites did not threaten Mr. Zelig with a State Bar complaint, Miller and TR chose to file a State Bar complaint against Mr. Zelig on their own, and Mr. Zelig’s declaration includes no statements that he was in fact threatened (in writing or orally) by Mr. Stites regarding a State Bar complaint. 

 

The Court finds Geragos v. Abelyan (2023) 88 Cal.App.5th 1005 instructive.  In that case, the Court of Appeal was left with the parties’ declarations, which resulted in a he-said-she-said conflict as to what was actually said regarding whether threats to file a State Bar complaint were made.  The Court found that “[t]his does not equate to conclusive evidence of extortion as a matter of law. ‘If ... a factual dispute exists about the legitimacy of the defendant's conduct, it cannot be resolved within the first step but must be raised by the plaintiff in connection with the plaintiff's burden to show a probability of prevailing on the merits.’ [Citation.]”  (Geragos v. Abelyan (2023) 88 Cal.App.5th 1005, 1031 [citing Flatley v. Mauro (2006) 39 Cal.4th 299, 316].) 

 

Thus, as framed by the pleadings, the Court finds that Mr. Stites has upheld his initial burden on the first prong with respect to the Fourth Cause of Action for IIED only regarding the alleged threat by Mr. Stites to report Mr. Zelig to the State Bar.

 

C.     Prong 2:  Probability of Prevailing on the Merits – Plaintiffs’ Shifted Burden  

 

For the reasons stated above, the Court finds that Mr. Stites has not upheld his initial burden on whether his speech or conduct arose from protected activity with respect to the Second and Third Causes of Action.  As such, the Court need not reach the second step of whether Plaintiffs can demonstrate the probability of prevailing on these claims. 

 

Thus, the Court only addresses the probability of prevailing on the merits with respect to the Fourth Cause of Action for IIED.

 

Plaintiffs argue that Mr. Stites, Miller, and TR do not state in their declarations when Miller and TR made the reports nor attach a copy of the State Bar complaint.  Mr. Zelig also argues that he has not received any notification that a complaint was made, which “places in further doubt the facially outrageous declarations of Stites, Miller, and TR.”  (Opp. at p.15.) 

 

However, as summarized above, Mr. Stites states that he did not threaten Mr. Zelig that he would be filing a State Bar complaint against him.  A review of Mr. Zelig’s declaration shows that Mr. Zelig did not make any affirmative statements that Mr. Stites did in fact make such threats.  Next, Miller and TR state that they chose to lodge a State Bar complaint against Mr. Zelig, which Mr. Zelig too does not deny with any affirmative statements.  Rather, he states in uncertain terms, “I may be wrong, but I do not believe Miller is telling the truth.”  (Zelig Decl., ¶19.)  While the Court is tasked with accepting as true all evidence favorable to Plaintiffs in evaluating the second prong, it also Plaintiffs’ burden to make an evidentiary showing with competent and admissible evidence.  Mr. Zelig’s unsubstantiated opinion that he believes Miller’s declaration statement (made under the penalty of perjury) that she decided to call the California State Bar and then file a complaint against Mr. Zelig to be false do not amount to competent evidence. 

 

Finally, Plaintiffs argue that Mr. Stites’ conduct amounts to extortion. 

 

In Flatley v. Mauro (2006) 39 Cal.4th 299, plaintiff (a well-known entertainer) sued defendant/attorney for civil extortion, IIED, and wrongful interference with economic advantage.  (Flatley, supra, 39 Cal.4th at 305.)  The plaintiff’s action was based on a demand letter defendant sent on behalf of his client, which defendant claimed was a prelitigation settlement offer and arose from his exercise of his constitutionally protected right to petition.  The defendant’s letter threatened to publicly accuse plaintiff of rape and report/accuse him of other unspecified violations of the law unless he “settled” by paying the defendant’s client (of which defendant would receive 40%); a “settlement of $100,000,000” awarded as punitive damages; and that defendant would conduct an in-depth investigation of his personal assets would be conducted and made public for the purpose of punitive damages (including immigration, social security issuances and use, and IRS and various state tax levies and information).)  The defendant also called, informing plaintiff that the price for his silence was at minimum $1 million.  (Id. at 307-311, 329-330.)  The trial court denied defendant’s anti-SLAPP motion, finding that defendant’s letter and telephone call constituted criminal extortion and extortionate speech was not constitutionally protected, which was affirmed by the Court of Appeal. 

 

The Supreme Court affirmed, stating that “section 425.16 cannot be invoked by a defendant whose assertedly protected activity is illegal as a matter of law and, for that reason, [is] not protected by constitutional guarantees of free speech and petition.”  (Id. at 317.)  A special motion to strike must be denied in the narrow circumstances where either the defendant concedes the illegality of its conduct or the illegality is conclusively shown by the evidence.  (Id. at 316.) “Extortion is not a constitutionally protected form of speech.”  (Id. at 328.)  The Supreme Court found that the defendant’s conduct was criminal extortion and was undeserving of protection under the anti-SLAPP statute.  (Id. at 326.)  It stated:

 

“Extortion is the obtaining of property from another, with his consent ... induced by a wrongful use of force or fear....” (Pen.Code, § 518.) Fear, for purposes of extortion “may be induced by a threat, either: [¶] ... [¶] 2. To accuse the individual threatened ... of any crime; or, [¶] 3. To expose, or impute to him ... any deformity, disgrace or crime[.]” (Pen.Code, § 519.) “Every person who, with intent to extort any money or other property from another, sends or delivers to any person any letter or other writing, whether subscribed or not, expressing or implying, or adapted to imply, any threat such as is specified in Section 519, is punishable in the same manner as if such money or property were actually obtained by means of such threat.” (Pen.Code, § 523.)

 

Extortion has been characterized as a paradoxical crime in that it criminalizes the making of threats that, in and of themselves, may not be illegal. “[I]n many blackmail cases the threat is to do something in itself perfectly legal, but that threat nevertheless becomes illegal when coupled with a demand for money.  (Philippine Export & Foreign Loan Guarantee Corp. v. Chuidian (1990) 218 Cal.App.3d 1058, 1079, 267 Cal.Rptr. 457.) …

 

…

 

Attorneys are not exempt from these principles in their professional conduct. Indeed, the Rules of Professional Conduct specifically prohibit attorneys from “threaten[ing] to present criminal, administration, or disciplinary charges to obtain an advantage in a civil dispute.” (Cal. Rules of Prof. Conduct, rule 5–100(A).)

 

(Id. at 326.)  The Supreme Court found that though the letter’s terms and the phone calls were couched in “legalese,” they constituted extortion because they threatened to accuse the plaintiff of, or impute to him, crimes and disgrace under Penal Code, § 519(2) and (3), such as rape and violations of immigration and tax law and the Social Security Act, which were unrelated to the alleged injury suffered by defendant’s client and exceeded his representation of that client.  (Id. at 330.) 

 

Penal Code, § 519 states:

 

Fear, such as will constitute extortion, may be induced by a threat of any of the following:

 

1. To do an unlawful injury to the person or property of the individual threatened or of a third person.

 

2. To accuse the individual threatened, or a relative of his or her, or a member of his or her family, of a crime.

 

3. To expose, or to impute to him, her, or them a deformity, disgrace, or crime.

 

4. To expose a secret affecting him, her, or them.

 

5. To report his, her, or their immigration status or suspected immigration status.

 

(Penal Code, § 519.) 

 

Here, Plaintiffs have not conclusively shown by the evidence that Mr. Stites’ conduct was illegal or amounted to extortion.  Unlike Flatley or Cohen, there is no evidence of letters, emails, or phone calls that amounted to Mr. Stites threatening any of the conduct in Penal Code, § 519.   Rather, as shown by Mr. Stites’ declaration, which is currently undisputed by Plaintiffs (though the Court notes that Plaintiffs intend to object to his declaration orally at the hearing), Mr. Stites did not threaten to file a claim and did not actually file a claim with the State Bar. 

 

Furthermore, the Court notes that Plaintiffs’ opposition papers do not discuss the basic elements of an IIED claim.  (See Opp. at pp.12-15.) 

 

The Court finds that Plaintiffs have not established their shifted burden of establishing the probability of prevailing on Mr. Zelig’s IIED claim.  As such, the motion is granted as to the IIED claim with respect to the State Bar allegations only.

 

Attorneys Fees

 

The Court will proactively address the issue of attorney’s fees.  In the event a defendant sought a fee award, the Court would be disinclined to grant the request for the reasons stated below:

 

A fee award is not required when the motion, though partially successful, was of no practical effect. (Moran v. Endres (2006) 135 Cal.App.4th 952, 955–956 [the trial court did not abuse its discretion when it denied the defendant's fees for an anti-SLAPP motion that challenged numerous tort claims brought by the plaintiff but succeeded in striking only a single cause of action for conspiracy].) “[A] party who partially prevails on an anti-SLAPP motion must generally be considered a prevailing party unless the results of the motion were so insignificant that the party did not achieve any practical benefit from bringing the motion. The determination whether a party prevailed on an anti-SLAPP motion lies within the broad discretion of a trial court.” (Mann v. Quality Old Time Service, Inc. 139 Cal.App.4th at p. 340; Lin v. City of Pleasanton (2009) 176 Cal.App.4th 408, 426).
