ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Henry Eli Villalta Aparicio, Juan Villalata, Handy Abdiel Villalta, Erwin Javier Villalta Aparicio, and Helsy Melissa Villalta Morazan (“Plaintiffs”) allege that they were tenants of the residential complex located at 838 North El Molino Ave, Apt. 8, in Pasadena, which was owned and/or managed by Massoud G. Tayyar and 838-840 N. El Molino LLC (“Defendants”).  (Compl., ¶¶1-3, 21.)  Plaintiffs allege they entered into a written lease agreement for Apartment 8 with Defendants in 2020.  (Id., ¶¶22, 24.)  Plaintiffs contend that Defendants engaged in wrongful conduct including intentionally and/or negligently failing to make repairs to the property, the common areas, and maintain the habitability of Apartment 8 and the property throughout Plaintiffs’ tenancy.  (Id., ¶28.)  Plaintiffs assert the unit and the property generally were unsafe, unsanitary, unhealthy, and uninhabitable and subject to substandard conditions, including: (a) dampness, moisture, and mold; (b) cockroach infestation; (c) bed bug infestation; (d) rodent infestation; (e) water leaks; (f) deteriorating or ineffective weatherproofing and/or waterproofing; (g) inadequate, defective, and unsafe plumbing conditions; (h) common areas in disrepair and posing a hazardous condition; (i) crumbling, cracked and/or deteriorating walls, ceilings, and/or flooring; and (j) bubbling paint.  (Id., ¶29.)   Plaintiffs allege that Defendants had actual and/or constructive notice of the defects, as Plaintiffs made multiple complaints via calls and texts to manager Susana, but Defendants failed to take timely or reasonable steps to abate or remedy the defects.  (Id., ¶¶30, 33-34.) 

 

The Complaint, filed April 28, 2026, alleges: (1) Negligence; (2) Tortious Breach of Implied Warranty of Habitability; (3) Breach of the Implied Warranty of Habitability; (4) Private Nuisance; (5) Breach of Covenant of Quiet Enjoyment; (6) Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (“IIED”); (7) Violation of the UCL; (8) Violation of Civil Code, § 1942; and (9) Violation of the Pasadena Fair and Equitable Housing Charter Amendment. 

 

MOTIONS ON CALENDAR:

 

On June 30, 2026, Defendants filed a Demurrer and Motion to Strike portions of the Complaint.  On August 28, 2026, Plaintiffs filed an opposition to the demurrer only.  On September 3, 2026, Defendants filed a reply regarding the demurrer only.

 

LEGAL STANDARD

 

A.     Demurrer

 

The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters. (C.C.P. § 430.30(a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal. 3d 311, 318.) A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) The only issue involved in a demurrer hearing is whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Id.)

 

A demurrer assumes the truth of all factual, material allegations properly pled in the challenged pleading. (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at p. 318.) No matter how unlikely or improbable, the plaintiff’s allegations must be accepted as true for the purpose of ruling on the demurrer. (Del E. Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.  App. 3d 593, 604.) But this does not include contentions; deductions; conclusions of fact or law alleged in the complaint; facts impossible in law; or allegations contrary to facts of which a court may take judicial notice.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at 318.)

 

Pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 430.10(e) and (f), the party against whom a complaint has been filed may demur to the pleading on the grounds that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, or that the pleading is uncertain, ambiguous and/or unintelligible. It is an abuse of discretion to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is a reasonable probability that the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal. 4th 1074, 1082.)

 

B.     Motion to Strike

 

Motions to strike are used to reach defects or objections to pleadings that are not challengeable by demurrer, such as words, phrases, and prayers for damages. (See C.C.P. §§ 435, 436, and 437.) The proper procedure to attack false allegations in a pleading is a motion to strike. (C.C.P. § 436(a).) In granting a motion to strike made under C.C.P. § 435, “[t]he court may, upon a motion made pursuant to Section 435 [notice of motion to strike whole or part of complaint], or at any time in its discretion, and upon terms it deems proper: (a) Strike out any irrelevant, false, or improper matter inserted in any pleading.” (C.C.P. § 436(a).) Irrelevant matters include immaterial allegations that are not essential to the claim or those not pertinent to or supported by an otherwise sufficient claim. (C.C.P. § 431.10.)

 

The court may also “[s]trike out all or any part of any pleading not drawn or filed in conformity with the laws of this state, a court rule, or an order of the court.” (C.C.P. § 436(b).)

 

MEET AND CONFER:

 

C.C.P. §§ 430.41(a) and 435.5(a) require that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the demurrer and/or motion to strike. Upon review, the Court finds the meet and confer requirements were met. (See Vardeh Demurrer Decl., ¶1; Vardeh MTS Decl., ¶1.) 

 

REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE:

 

With the moving papers, Defendants request judicial notice of Exhibits: (A) the Complaint – Unlawful Detainer filed May 18, 2026 in Case No. 26NNCV03915 (“UD Action”); (B) the Complaint filed May 20, 2026 in Case No. 26NNCV03962 (“Civil Action”); and (C) the Pasadena Municipal Code, Article XVIII.  The request is granted.  (Evid. Code, § 452(b), (d).) 

 

DEMURRER ANALYSIS:

 

Defendants demur to the Sixth Cause of Action for IIED on the ground that it fails to allege sufficient facts to constitute a cause of action. 

 

The elements of intentional infliction of emotional distress (“IIED”) are: (1) outrageous conduct by the defendant; (2) the defendant’s intention of causing or reckless disregard of the probability of causing emotional distress; (3) the plaintiff suffered severe or extreme emotional distress; and (4) the plaintiff’s injuries were actually and proximately caused by the defendant’s outrageous conduct.  (Vasquez v. Franklin Mgmt. Real Estate Fund, Inc. (2013) 222 Cal.App.4th 819, 832.)  In order to avoid a demurrer, the plaintiff must allege with great specificity, the acts which she believes are so extreme as to exceed all bounds of behavior usually tolerated in a civilized community.  (Id.)

 

Conduct to be outrageous must be so extreme as to exceed all bounds of behavior usually tolerated in a civilized community.  (Christensen v. Superior Court (1991) 54 Cal.3d 868, 903.)  In addition, the outrageous conduct must be of a nature which is especially calculated to cause, and does cause, mental distress of a very serious kind.  (Id.)  “Although emotional distress may consist of any highly unpleasant mental reaction such as fright, grief, shame, humiliation, embarrassment, anger, chagrin, disappointment or worry [citation], to make out a claim, the plaintiff must prove that emotional distress was severe and not trivial or transient.”  (Wong v. Tai Jing (2010) 189 Cal.App.4th 1354, 1376.)  Such distress must be “of such substantial quality or enduring quality that no reasonable person in civilized society should be expected to endure it.”  (Potter v. Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. (1993) 6 Cal.4th 965, 1004.)

 

In the Sixth Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants’ acts and omissions, including inducing Plaintiffs to rent a dwelling containing defects, which Defendants had intentionally failed to identify, abate, and repair in an effective manner, was outrageous.  (Compl., ¶86.)  They allege “Defendants knew that intentionally failing to identify, abate, and repair the housing defects would expose Plaintiffs to deplorable conditions including exposure to mold mycotoxins and vermin allergens. This was intentionally done to cause harm to Plaintiffs as Defendants knew that a reasonable tenant, including Plaintiffs, would suffer severe emotional distress and Plaintiff did suffer such distress in having to live with such defects and uninhabitable conditions. Despite this knowledge, Defendants took no steps to change their actions.”  (Id.)  Plaintiffs contend Defendants’ conduct caused Plaintiff to suffer severe emotional distress, Defendants acted with reckless disregard of the probability of causing Plaintiffs severe emotional distress, and Defendants intentionally failed to repair and maintain the property in an attempt to save money and increase their cash flow.  (Id., ¶¶87-88.)  Plaintiffs assert Defendants’ conduct was a substantial factor in causing and that Plaintiffs suffered severe emotional distress, as well as respiratory issues, skin allergies, runny nose, watery eyes, coughing, emotional distress, lack of sleep, stress, general discomfort, annoyance, and inability to quietly enjoy their home, and related physical symptoms or bodily injury due to the mold growth in the property. (Id., ¶89.)   

 

Defendants argue that Plaintiffs use the word “intentional” without supporting facts to show that Defendants acted intentionally, as opposed to negligently. 

 

The Complaint alleges that “Plaintiffs made actual complaints and attempted to make complaints to Defendants and/or their agents shortly after discovering the various defects mentioned herein, including but not limited to, calls and text messages to manager Susana (last name unknown) on February 15, 2024, February 17, 2024, March 27, 2024, July 19, 2024, July 31, 2024, August 1, 2024, and manager Diana Monotono on June 11, 2025, June 18, 2025, and July 28, 2025. Discovery is ongoing.”  (Compl., ¶33.)  Plaintiffs alleged that despite making such complaints, Defendants intentionally ignored or refused Plaintiffs’ requests to make repairs.  (Id., ¶34.) 

 

The Complaint’s allegations do not rise to the level of outrageous conduct.  While Plaintiffs allege that Defendants were notified of issues and ignored or refused Plaintiffs’ request to make repairs, this does not amount to conduct that is so extreme as to exceed all bounds of behavior usually tolerated in a civilized community. 

 

The demurrer to the Sixth Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend. 

 

MOTION TO STRIKE ANALYSIS:

 

Defendants move to strike allegations for: (1) punitive damages at paragraphs 43 (First Cause of Action), 57 (Second Cause of Action), 74 (Fourth Cause of Action), 83 (Fifth Cause of Action), and 90 (Sixth Cause of Action), and the Prayer for Relief at paragraphs 2 (23:11 for the First Cause of Action), 5 (23:18 for the Second Cause of Action), 10 (24:02 for the Fourth Cause of Action), 8 (24:8 for the Fifth Cause of Action), 16 (24:15 for the Sixth Cause of Action); and (2) treble damages in the Prayer for Relief at paragraph 24 (25:09 for the Ninth Cause of Action). 

 

A.     Punitive Damages

 

A complaint including a request for punitive damages must include allegations showing that the plaintiff is entitled to an award of punitive damages.  (Clauson v. Superior Court (1998) 67 Cal.App.4th 1253, 1255.)  A claim for punitive damages cannot be pleaded generally and allegations that a defendant acted "with oppression, fraud and malice" toward plaintiff are insufficient legal conclusions to show that the plaintiff is entitled to an award of punitive damages.  (Brousseau v. Jarrett (1977) 73 Cal.App.3d 864, 872.)  Specific factual allegations are required to support a claim for punitive damages.  (Id.)

 

Civil Code § 3294 authorizes a plaintiff to obtain an award of punitive damages when there is clear and convincing evidence that the defendant engaged in malice, oppression, or fraud.  Section 3294(c) defines the terms in the following manner:

 

(1) "Malice" means conduct which is intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff or despicable conduct which is carried on by the defendant with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others.

 

(2) "Oppression" means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person's rights.

 

(3) "Fraud" means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention on the part of the defendant of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. 

 

(Civ. Code, § 3294(c).)

 

For example, the First Cause of Action for Negligence alleges in paragraph 43:

 

Defendants’ conduct described above was willful, wanton, intentional, despicable, malicious, and initiated with malice and with the intent to knowingly take advantage of, oppress, and injure Plaintiffs. Defendants at all times acted with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights of safety of Plaintiffs. Defendants were at all times aware that there was a high probability that their intentional and/or negligent failure to repair and maintain the Property would injure Plaintiffs and cause them personal injury, emotional distress and property damage. Plaintiffs are therefore entitled to an award of punitive and exemplary damages under and pursuant to Civil Code, Section 3294 and Taylor v. Superior Court (1979) 24 Cal.3d 890.

 

(Compl., ¶43.)  The other punitive damages paragraphs are similar in form. 

 

The Court has reviewed the Complaint’s allegations and finds that the punitive damages allegations are not alleged with the requisite particularity.  As currently alleged, they are conclusory regarding allegations for malice and oppression.   The motion to strike the allegations for punitive damages is granted with leave to amend.

 

B.     Treble Damages

 

In the Ninth Cause of Action, Plaintiffs seek treble damages for a landlord’s violation of the Fair and Equitable Charter Amendment.  (See Compl., ¶111.) 

 

The Pasadena Municipal Code, § 1817(b) states:

 

Civil Remedies. A Tenant may bring a civil suit in the courts of the state alleging that a Landlord has violated any of the provisions of this Article or the regulations promulgated hereunder, including that the Landlord has demanded, accepted, received, or retained a payment or payments in excess of the lawful Rent. In a civil suit, a Landlord found to violate this Article shall be liable to the Tenant for all actual damages, including but not limited to the damages described in Subsection (a) herein. A prevailing Tenant in a civil action brought to enforce this Article shall be awarded reasonable attorney’s fees and costs as determined by the court. Additionally, upon a showing that the Landlord has acted willfully or with oppression, fraud, or malice, the Tenant shall be awarded treble damages. No administrative remedy need be exhausted prior to filing suit pursuant to this subsection.

 

(Def.’s RJN, Ex. C at p. 40 [Pasadena Municipal Code, § 1817(b)].) 

 

Defendants argue that the standard in Pasadena Municipal Code, § 1817(b) is essentially identical to that of Civil Code, § 3294, which require as showing of oppression, fraud, or malice. 

 

For the same reasons above, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ allegations in the Ninth Cause of Action do not rise to the level of showing that Defendants acted with malice, oppression, and/or fraud to warrant treble damages.  Thus, the motion to strike the treble damages allegations is granted with leave to amend.

 

--- 

 

RULING:

ORDER 

 

Defendants Massoud G. Tayyar and 838-840 N. El Molino LLC’s Demurrer and Motion to Strike came on regularly for hearing on September 11, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows:  

 

The Demurrer to the complaint iS SUSTAINED WITH 20 DAYS’ LEAVE TO AMEND AS TO THE SIXTH CAUSE OF ACTION.

 

THE MOTION TO STRIKE THE PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND TREBLE DAMAGES ALLEGATIONS IS GRANTED WITH 20 DAYS’ LEAVE TO AMEND.

Case Number: 26NNCV05103    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

DEMURRER

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 26NNCV05103

 

MP:     Defendant GOR Enterprises, Inc. dba Paradise Pastry & Cafe

RP:      Plaintiff Alisa Galstyan

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Alisa Galstyan (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on July 4, 2024, GOR Enterprises, Inc. dba Paradise Pastry & Cafe (“Defendant”) poured scalding hot tea into defective paper cups with an unsecured, defective lid, placed them on a plastic tray, and handed them to Plaintiff to carry to her seat.  Plaintiff alleges that the hot tea caused thermal degradation of the paper cups/lids, such that their structural integrity was compromised, causing the seam to open and tea to pour onto the tray.  Plaintiff contends the force of the tea spilling onto the tray, caused the other cup of tea to fall over, spilling hot tea from both cups onto Plaintiff, causing her to sustain injuries. 

 

The Complaint, filed June 26, 2026, alleges: (1) General Negligence; (2) Premises Liability; and (3) Products Liability.

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On August 5, 2026, Defendant filed a Demurrer to the Complaint.  On August 25, 2026, Plaintiff filed an opposition.  On September 2, 2026, Defendant filed a reply. 

 

LEGAL STANDARD

 

The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters. (C.C.P. § 430.30(a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal. 3d 311, 318.) A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) The only issue involved in a demurrer hearing is whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Id.)

 

A demurrer assumes the truth of all factual, material allegations properly pled in the challenged pleading. (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at p. 318.) No matter how unlikely or improbable, the plaintiff’s allegations must be accepted as true for the purpose of ruling on the demurrer. (Del E. Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.  App. 3d 593, 604.) But this does not include contentions; deductions; conclusions of fact or law alleged in the complaint; facts impossible in law; or allegations contrary to facts of which a court may take judicial notice.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at 318.)

 

Pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 430.10(e) and (f), the party against whom a complaint has been filed may demur to the pleading on the grounds that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, or that the pleading is uncertain, ambiguous and/or unintelligible. It is an abuse of discretion to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is a reasonable probability that the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal. 4th 1074, 1082.)

 

MEET AND CONFER:

 

C.C.P. §§ 430.41(a) and 435.5(a) require that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the demurrer and/or motion to strike. Upon review, the Court finds the meet and confer requirements were met. (See Motooka Decl., ¶¶3-6, Exs. A-B.) 

 

ANALYSIS:

 

Defendant demurs to the Second Cause of Action for Premises Liability, arguing it fails to allege sufficient facts to constitute a cause of action against it, it is duplicative of the First Cause of Action for General Negligence, and it is uncertain. 

 

The elements of a premises liability claim and negligence claim are the same: a legal duty of care, breach of that duty, and proximate cause resulting in injury.  (Kesner v. Superior Court (2016) 1 Cal.5th 1132, 1158.) 

 

The allegations of the First Cause of Action are summarized under the “ALLEGATIONS” portion above.  Plaintiff further contends in the General Negligence Cause of Action that by serving tea that was too hot for human consumption into a defective paper cup with defective, unsecured lids, Defendants created a dangerous condition that resulted in Plaintiff sustaining severe burns.  She alleges that either the cup or the glue was made from materials that could not withstand the hot tea.  She alleges Defendant was negligent in brewing, packaging, serving, inspecting, managing, supervising, controlling and/or operating the premises; in hiring, training, supervising, controlling, and/or monitoring employees and agents responsible for the brewing, preparing, packaging, serving hot liquids and the inspections, supervision, control, and operations; in failing to provide service of hot liquids that were safe and free from harmful and injurious conditions, that are safe and reasonably fit for human consumption.  (Compl. at p.4.) 

 

In the Second Cause of Action for Premises Liability, Plaintiff alleges that she sustained injuries when Defendant negligently served her scalding hot tea in a defective cup with an unsecured, defective lid.  She alleges the tea was too hot for human consumption and compromised the structural integrity of the defective paper cup and lid, causing the seam to break open and give way under the tea’s heat.  She contends this caused the tea to pour out onto the tray, knocking over the other cup of overly hot tea and onto Plaintiff. She alleges that either the cup or the glue was made from materials that could not withstand the hot tea, such that the materials were not of adequate quality for the intended use.  She asserts that Defendant’s negligence created a dangerous condition on its property located at1825 West Glenoaks, Glendale, CA 91201.  She is informed and believes that the hazardous, dangerous conditions were caused by Defendant and/or existed for a sufficient time prior to the incident for Defendant to have corrected, removed, and/or warned Plaintiff of the existence of said conditions.  (Compl. at p.5.) 

 

While Plaintiff alleges that the subject incident occurred on Defendant’s premises, Plaintiff has not alleged facts that there was a physical condition of the premises itself that caused her injury. (See Kinsman v. Unocal Corp. (2005) 37 Cal.4th 659, 673 [“A possessor of land is subject to liability for physical harm caused to his invitees by a condition on the land if, but only if, he [¶] (a) knows or by the exercise of reasonable care would discover the condition, and should realize that it involves an unreasonable risk of harm to such invitees, and [¶] (b) should expect that they will not discover or realize the danger, or will fail to protect themselves against it, and [¶] (c) fails to exercise reasonable care to protect them against the danger.”] [quoting the Restatement of Torts Second, section 343].)  At most, Plaintiff alleges that a cup and/or lid were defective or that Defendant allowed service of scalding hot tea in the cup atop a tray, but she has not alleged any facts that there was anything dangerous about the conditions of the premises, such as uneven or cracked flooring, a wet substance on the floor, slippery floors, etc.  Thus, the demurrer is sustained on the ground that the Premises Liability claim fails to allege sufficient facts against Defendant.

 

Next, as currently worded, the Premises Liability claim is duplicative of the General Negligence claim, as it relies on the same facts that the tea was scalding hot and the cup/lid were defective in some way.  This too will be a ground to sustain the demurrer.

 

The demurrer to the Second Cause of Action is sustained.  As this is Plaintiff’s first attempt at the pleadings, the Court will allow leave to amend.

The Demurrer to the SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION IN THE complaint iS SUSTAINED WITH 20 DAYS’ LEAVE TO AMEND.

Case Number: 26PDUD01363    Hearing Date: September 11, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

SEPTEMBER 11, 2026

MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 26PDUD01363

 

MP:     Defendant Omayra Mangual

RP:      No opposition received (oral opposition permitted for UD action)  

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at BurDeptA@LACourt.ca.gov or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

On May 4, 2026, Glen Louise, LLC (“Plaintiff”) filed an Unlawful Detainer Complaint against Omayra Mangual (“Defendant”) regarding the premises located at 308 N. Louise Street, #2, Glendale, CA 91206.  The parties entered into a written lease agreement on December 10, 2021.  Defendant was served with a 3-day notice to pay rent or quit on March 26, 2026, which expired on March 31, 2026.  Plaintiff seeks possession of the premises, costs and reasonable attorney’s fees, past-due rent of $3,090.33, forfeiture of the agreement, and damages at $51.50 per day from April 1, 2026.  

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On August 4, 2026, Defendant (a self-represented litigant) filed a Motion for Summary Judgment.  Pursuant to CRC Rule 3.1351(b), opposition and reply briefs to a motion for summary judgment may be made orally at the time of the hearing.  If a party seeks to have a written opposition considered in advance of the hearing, the written opposition must be filed and served on or before the court day before the hearing; the court may consider a written opposition filed later.  (CRC Rule 3.1351(c).) 

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

The function of a motion for summary judgment or adjudication is to allow a determination as to whether an opposing party cannot show evidentiary support for a pleading or claim and to enable an order of summary dismissal without the need for trial. (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843.) C.C.P. § 437c(c) “requires the trial judge to grant summary judgment if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.”  (Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119.)

 

As to each claim as framed by the complaint, the defendant moving for summary judgment must satisfy the initial burden of proof by presenting facts to negate an essential element, or to establish a defense. (C.C.P. § 437c(p)(2); Scalf v. D. B. Log Homes, Inc. (2005) 128 Cal.App.4th 1510, 1520.)  Courts “liberally construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment and resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.”  (Dore v. Arnold Worldwide, Inc. (2006) 39 Cal.4th 384, 389.) Once the defendant has met that burden, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to show that a triable issue of one or more material facts exists as to that cause of action or a defense thereto.  To establish a triable issue of material fact, the party opposing the motion must produce substantial responsive evidence. (Sangster v. Paetkau (1998) 68 Cal.App.4th 151, 166.)

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

Defendant moves for summary judgment on the Complaint, arguing the following Issues: (1) the three-day notice on which the Complaint is based is void because it overstates the rent due; and (2) the verified Complaint falsely alleges that the tenancy is exempt from the Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (Civil Code, §§ 1946.2, 1947.12), when Plaintiff’s own written lease affirmatively states that the tenancy is subject to that Act. 

 

A.     Issue 1 – The Three-Day Notice

 

C.C.P. § 1161(2) states:

 

A tenant of real property, for a term less than life, or the executor or administrator of the tenant's estate heretofore qualified and now acting or hereafter to be qualified and act, is guilty of unlawful detainer: …

 

2. When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due, the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent payment shall be made, and, if payment may be made personally, the usual days and hours that person will be available to receive the payment (provided that, if the address does not allow for personal delivery, then it shall be conclusively presumed that upon the mailing of any rent or notice to the owner by the tenant to the name and address provided, the notice or rent is deemed received by the owner on the date posted, if the tenant can show proof of mailing to the name and address provided by the owner), or the number of an account in a financial institution into which the rental payment may be made, and the name and street address of the institution (provided that the institution is located within five miles of the rental property), or if an electronic funds transfer procedure has been previously established, that payment may be made pursuant to that procedure, or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant.

 

The notice may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due. In all cases of tenancy upon agricultural lands, if the tenant has held over and retained possession for more than 60 days after the expiration of the term without any demand of possession or notice to quit by the landlord or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, the tenant shall be deemed to be holding by permission of the landlord or successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, and shall be entitled to hold under the terms of the lease for another full year, and shall not be guilty of an unlawful detainer during that year, and the holding over for that period shall be taken and construed as a consent on the part of a tenant to hold for another year.

 

(C.C.P. § 1161(2).)

 

Pursuant to section 1161(2), a “valid three-day pay rent or quit notice is a prerequisite to an unlawful detainer action. [Citations.] Because of the summary nature of an unlawful detainer action, a notice is valid only if the lessor strictly complies with the statutorily mandated notice requirements. [Citation.]”  (Bevill v. Zoura (1994) 27 Cal.App.4th 694, 697 [citations omitted].)  This subsection requires that the three-day notice contain “the amount which is due” and a “notice which demands rent in excess of the amount due does not satisfy this requirement.”  (Id.)  “This rule ensures that a landlord will not be entitled to regain possession in an unlawful detainer action unless the tenant has had the opportunity to pay the delinquent rent.”  (Id.)

 

Defendant provides the following material facts regarding Issue 1 (rent overstatement).  Defendant occupies the residential premises at 308 N. Louise Street, #2 (the “Premises”) under a written lease dated December 10, 2021, at a monthly rent of $1,450.00 at the time.  (Def.’s Fact 1.)  On March 6, 2026, Plaintiff served Defendant with a Three-Day Notice to Pay Rent or Quit demanding $3,090.33 (“First Notice”).  (Id. at 2.)  On March 26, 2026, Plaintiff served Defendant with a second Three-Day Notice to Pay Rent or Quit demanding the same amount (“Second Notice”).  (Id. at 3.)  The Second Notice states on its face: “THIS NOTICE SUPERSEDES ALL PREVIOUS NOTICES.”  (Id. at 4.)  Both notices itemize a January 2026 “Amount Due” of $0.33.  (Id. at 5.)  Defendant paid the January 2026 rent in full and no January 2026 balance, including the $0.33, was owed.  (Id. at 5.)  Defendant contends the Second Notice demanded rent she did not owe.  (Id. at 6.) 

 

Both the March 6, 2026 and March 26, 2026 Notices seek the following: (1) $0.33 for the 1/1/2026 – 1/31/2026 rental period; (2) $1,545.00 for the 2/1/2026 – 2/28/2026 rental period; and (3) $1,545.00 for the 3/1/2026 – 3/31/2026 rental period, for a total of $3,090.33.  (Def.’s Decl., Ex. A.) 

 

With respect to the January 2026 rent, Defendant provides a text message exchange (from “Diana” at phone number +1(323)613-3958) showing the $1,637.70 amount she was directed to pay (which was $1,545 in January’s rent + $92.70 for January’s late fee) by January 21, 2026 and a check showing that Defendant made a check out to Glen Louise, LLC for $1,637.70 dated January 17, 2026.  (Def.’s Decl., Ex. A.) 

 

Defendant has upheld her initial burden in showing that she paid the January 2026 rent as requested, such that the $0.33 rental amount requested in both Notices for January 2026 was overstated. 

 

Thus, the burden shifts to Plaintiff to raise a triable issue of material fact.  The Court is not in receipt of a written opposition.  However, as noted above, this is an unlawful detainer action such that Plaintiff may present oral arguments at the hearing.

 

Based on Defendant’s moving papers, the Court is inclined to grant the motion on Issue 1. 

 

B.     Issue 2 – The Tenant Protection Act of 2019

 

Defendant provides the following material facts regarding Issue 2 (Tenant Protection Act).  The Premises are located within a multi-unit residential building (approximately 20 units) constructed in or about 1949.  (Def.’s Fact 8.)  Defendant has continuously and lawfully occupied the Premises for more than 12 months.  (Id. at 9.) Defendant contends by reason of the building’s age, size, and residential use, and Defendant’s length of occupancy, the tenancy is subject to Civil Code §§ 1946.2 and 1947.12 and does not fall within any statutory exemption under sections 1946.2(e) or 1947.12(d).  (Id. at 10.) 

 

Section 35 of the parties’ lease (“Assembly Bill 1482 Disclosures”) directs the parties to “Check the applicable provision” and presents two alternatives, wherein: (a) Plaintiff left blank provision stating the property is “not subject” to Sections 1947.12 and 1946.2, and instead (b) checked the provision stating that California law limits rent increases (§ 1947.12) and requires a statement of cause to terminate (§ 1946.2).  (Id. at 11-12.)  Specifically, this section states:

 

[X] California law limits the amount your rent can be increased. See Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code for more information. California law also provides that after all of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months or more or at least one of the tenants has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 24 months or more, a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy. See Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code for more information.

 

(Def.’s Decl., Ex. C [Lease at § 35].) 

 

Plaintiff's verified Complaint alleges at Item 7a, under penalty of perjury, that the tenancy is “not subject to the Tenant Protection Act of 2019,” stating the claimed exemption as “GRSO.”  (Def.’s Fact 13.)  Defendant contends that “GRSO” is not a recognized statutory exemption under Civil Code section 1946.2(e), and the City of Glendale does not maintain an independent rent-control ordinance supplying such an exemption.  (Id. at 14.)  He claims because the tenancy is covered, the written notice was required to state just cause for termination, but the notice stated none.  (Id. at 15.)

 

Defendant has upheld her initial burden in showing that based on the Lease agreement, her tenancy at the subject property is subject to the Tenant Protection Act.  Defendant entered the Lease in December 2021, such that her tenancy exceeded 12 months.  Civil Code, § 1946.2(e) states that the section does not apply for certain types of residential properties, such as transient/tourist hotel occupancy; housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, etc.; dormitories; etc. Plaintiff’s Complaint and the Lease agreement do not state that the subject property qualifies for an exemption under this subsection.  Furthermore, Plaintiff generally cited the GRSO in the Complaint, but did not provide any specific citation, quote any provision, or show how it provides an exemption to the Tenant Protection Act.

 

Thus, the burden shifts to Plaintiff to raise a triable issue of material fact.  The Court is not in receipt of a written opposition.  However, as noted above, this is an unlawful detainer action such that Plaintiff may present oral arguments at the hearing.

 

Based on Defendant’s moving papers, the Court is inclined to grant the motion on Issue 2.
